docs.concept: Hybrid decoupling: SQS / SWF with workers on EC2 and on-premises
docs.tests: Knowing which AWS services decouple application components and can be used by both EC2 and on-premises servers.
docs.expected: SQS (message queue) and SWF (workflow with activity workers that can run anywhere). Triggers: "decoupled architecture" + "on-premises and AWS" → SQS / SWF — both are public API endpoints reachable from anywhere.
docs.why_not: RDS and DynamoDB are databases, not decoupling services; VPC peering only connects VPCs (not on-prem) and is networking, not decoupling.

question.stem:
A company has two On-Demand EC2 instances inside the Virtual Private Cloud in the same Availability Zone but are deployed to different subnets. One EC2 instance is running a database and the other EC2 instance a web application that connects with the database. You need to ensure that these two instances can communicate with each other for the system to work properly.
What are the things you have to check so that these EC2 instances can communicate inside the VPC? (Select TWO.)
options: Check if both instances are the same instance class.
Check the Network ACL if it allows communication between the two subnets.
Check if all security groups are set to allow the application host to communicate to the database on the right port and protocol.
Ensure that the EC2 instances are in the same Placement Group.
Check if the default route is set to a NAT instance or Internet Gateway (IGW) for them to communicate.
question.explanation: Every VPC route table has an implicit local route, so subnets in the same VPC can already reach each other — routing isn't the problem. Traffic between subnets is filtered by two layers: the Network ACLs of both subnets (stateless — allow the DB port inbound and ephemeral ports for replies) and the security groups (the DB instance's SG must allow the DB port from the app instance or its SG). Instance class and placement groups don't affect connectivity; NAT/IGW routes are only for traffic leaving the VPC.

docs.concept: VPC: intra-VPC connectivity = local route + SG + NACL
docs.tests: Knowing what controls traffic between subnets of the same VPC: security groups and network ACLs, not routing to NAT/IGW.
docs.expected: Check the NACLs between the two subnets and the security groups (DB SG allows the app on the DB port/protocol). Triggers: "same VPC", "different subnets", "can communicate" → SG + NACL; the local route already exists.
docs.why_not: Instance class and placement groups have nothing to do with reachability; NAT/IGW are only for traffic to the internet — the implicit local route handles intra-VPC traffic.

question.stem:
A company has developed public APIs hosted in Amazon EC2 instances behind an Elastic Load Balancer. The APIs will be used by various clients from respective on-premises data centers. A Solutions Architect received a report that the web service clients can only access trusted IP addresses whitelisted on the web service’s firewalls.
What should be done to accomplish the above requirement?
options: Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution whose origin points to the private IP addresses of your web servers.
Associate an Elastic IP address to an Application Load Balancer.
Associate an Elastic IP address to a Network Load Balancer.
Configure General Purpose SSD volumes on the load balancer nodes to provide static IP addresses.
question.explanation: Clients' firewalls only allow whitelisted destination IPs, so the API endpoint needs fixed IP addresses. A Network Load Balancer supports assigning one Elastic IP per enabled AZ (subnet mapping), giving static IPs clients can whitelist. An ALB's IPs change as it scales and it cannot take an Elastic IP (put an NLB in front of the ALB or use Global Accelerator if L7 features are needed). CloudFront can't use private IPs as a custom origin (origins must be publicly reachable) and its own edge IPs are numerous and changing. EBS/gp2/gp3 volumes are storage — they have nothing to do with IP addresses, and you can't configure load balancer nodes.

docs.concept: ELB: NLB with Elastic IPs for client IP whitelisting
docs.tests: Knowing which load balancer can have static Elastic IPs so clients can whitelist the endpoint.
docs.expected: Associate Elastic IPs with a Network Load Balancer (one per AZ). Triggers: "whitelist / allowlist IPs on firewall", "static IP" + load balancer → NLB with EIP (or Global Accelerator for 2 anycast IPs).
docs.why_not: ALB can't have an Elastic IP (its IPs change); CloudFront can't point to private IPs and its edge IPs aren't fixed; SSD volumes are storage, unrelated to IPs.

question.stem:
A startup has multiple AWS accounts that are assigned to its development teams. Since the company is projected to grow rapidly, the management wants to consolidate all of its AWS accounts into a multi-account setup. To simplify the login process on the AWS accounts, the management wants to utilize its existing directory service for user authentication
Which combination of actions should a solutions architect recommend to meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)
options: Create Service Control Policies (SCP) in the organization to manage the child accounts. Configure AWS IAM Identity Center (AWS Single Sign-On) to use AWS Directory Service.

On the master account, use AWS Organizations to create a new organization with all features turned on. Enable the organization’s external authentication and point it to use the company’s directory service.
On the master account, use AWS Organizations to create a new organization with all features turned on. Invite the child accounts to this new organization.
Create an identity pool on Amazon Cognito and configure it to use the company’s directory service. Configure AWS IAM Identity Center (AWS Single Sign-On) to accept Cognito authentication.
Configure AWS IAM Identity Center (AWS Single Sign-On) for the organization and integrate it with the company’s directory service using the Active Directory Connector
question.explanation: Account consolidation = AWS Organizations: create an organization with all features in the management account (required for IAM Identity Center and SCPs) and invite the existing accounts into it. Sign-in via the existing directory = IAM Identity Center connected to the on-prem AD through AD Connector (a proxy; users stay in the corporate AD). An SCP restricts permissions, it is not authentication, and "use AWS Directory Service" without AD Connector does not link to the existing directory. Organizations has no "external authentication" feature. Cognito identity pools are for application users (B2C); Identity Center does not accept Cognito as an identity source.

docs.concept: IAM Identity Center + Organizations: multi-account SSO via AD Connector
docs.tests: Combining two steps: consolidating accounts with Organizations (all features, invite) and workforce SSO via IAM Identity Center with the existing directory.
docs.expected: Organizations with all features + invite the accounts; IAM Identity Center integrated with the corporate AD via AD Connector. Triggers: "consolidate accounts / multi-account" → Organizations; "existing directory service for login" → Identity Center + AD Connector.
docs.why_not: SCPs govern permissions, not sign-in; "external authentication" does not exist in Organizations; Cognito is for application customers, not workforce access to accounts.

question.stem: An accounting application uses an Amazon RDS database configured with RDS Multi-AZ to improve availability. What would happen to RDS if the primary database instance fails?
options: The IP address of the primary DB instance is switched to the standby DB instance.
A new database instance is created in the standby Availability Zone.
The primary database instance will reboot.
The canonical name record (CNAME) is switched from the primary to standby instance.
question.explanation: On primary failure, RDS Multi-AZ automatically fails over by flipping the DB endpoint's DNS CNAME record to point at the standby, which is promoted to primary (typically 60–120 s). The application keeps using the same endpoint name; it only needs to reconnect (and respect DNS TTL). IP addresses are not moved between instances — primary and standby have different IPs in different AZs. RDS doesn't create a brand-new instance to serve traffic — the already-synchronized standby takes over (a replacement standby is provisioned afterwards). A reboot of the failed primary isn't the failover mechanism.

docs.concept: RDS Multi-AZ: failover flips the endpoint's DNS CNAME to the standby
docs.tests: Knowing the mechanism of RDS Multi-AZ failover: the DNS CNAME of the endpoint is switched to the standby.
docs.expected: The CNAME of the DB endpoint is switched from the primary to the standby (promoted to primary). Triggers: "what happens when the primary fails" in Multi-AZ → CNAME flip, same endpoint.
docs.why_not: IPs aren't moved (different AZ/subnet); the existing synchronous standby takes over — no new instance serves traffic; rebooting the primary isn't failover.

question.stem: An online events registration system is hosted in AWS and uses ECS to host its front-end tier and an RDS configured with Multi-AZ for its database tier. What are the events that will make Amazon RDS automatically perform a failover to the standby replica? (Select TWO.)
options: Loss of availability in primary Availability Zone
Storage failure on secondary DB instance
Storage failure on primary
In the event of Read Replica failure
Compute unit failure on secondary DB instance
question.explanation: RDS Multi-AZ fails over automatically when the PRIMARY becomes unavailable: loss of availability in the primary AZ, loss of network connectivity to the primary, compute unit failure on the primary, storage failure on the primary. Failover also happens during planned events (OS patching / instance class change on the primary, manual reboot with failover). Failures on the secondary (standby) don't trigger failover — RDS simply replaces the standby, the primary keeps serving. Read Replicas are separate, asynchronously replicated instances; their failure has nothing to do with Multi-AZ failover.

docs.concept: RDS Multi-AZ: what triggers automatic failover (primary-side failures only)
docs.tests: Knowing which events make RDS Multi-AZ fail over to the standby: failures of the primary, not of the standby or read replicas.
docs.expected: Loss of availability in the primary AZ and storage failure on the primary. Rule: anything wrong with the PRIMARY (AZ outage, network loss, compute failure, storage failure, patching/instance type change, reboot with failover) → failover.
docs.why_not: Storage/compute failure on the secondary → RDS just replaces the standby, no failover; Read Replica failure is unrelated to Multi-AZ.

question.stem:
A company has an enterprise web application hosted on Amazon ECS Docker containers that use an Amazon FSx for Lustre filesystem for its high-performance computing workloads. The application uses AWS X-Ray to trace requests across its containerized services. A warm standby environment is running in another AWS Region for disaster recovery.
A solutions architect was assigned to design a system that will automatically route the live traffic to the disaster recovery (DR) environment only in the event that the primary application stack experiences an outage.
What should the Architect do to satisfy this requirement?
options: Set up a failover routing policy configuration in Amazon Route 53 by adding a health check on the primary service endpoint. Configure Route 53 to direct the DNS queries to the secondary record when the primary resource is unhealthy. Configure the network access control list and the route table to allow Route 53 to send requests to the endpoints specified in the health checks. Enable the `Evaluate Target Health` option by setting it to `Yes`.

Set up an Amazon EventBridge rule to monitor the primary Amazon Route 53 DNS endpoint and create a custom AWS Lambda function. Execute the `ChangeResourceRecordSets` API call using the function to initiate the failover to the secondary DNS record.

Set up a Weighted routing policy configuration in Amazon Route 53 by adding health checks on both the primary stack and the DR environment. Configure the network access control list and the route table to allow Route 53 to send requests to the endpoints specified in the health checks. Enable the `Evaluate Target Health` option by setting it to `Yes`.

Set up an Amazon CloudWatch Alarm to monitor the primary Amazon Route 53 DNS endpoint and create a custom AWS Lambda function. Execute the `ChangeResourceRecordSets` API call using the function to initiate the failover to the secondary DNS record.
question.explanation: Route 53 failover routing is built for active-passive DR: a primary record with a health check and a secondary record pointing to the DR Region. When the health check marks the primary unhealthy, Route 53 answers DNS queries with the secondary record automatically; when it recovers, traffic returns. The health checkers must be able to reach the endpoint (allow Route 53 health-checker IP ranges in NACLs/security groups), and with alias records to ELB 'Evaluate Target Health = Yes' makes the record inherit the target's health. Weighted routing splits traffic across both stacks all the time — it doesn't send traffic to DR 'only' on outage. EventBridge/CloudWatch + Lambda calling ChangeResourceRecordSets re-implements failover with custom code — more overhead and more failure points than the native feature.

docs.concept: Route 53 failover routing: active/passive with health checks
docs.tests: Choosing native Route 53 failover routing with health checks for active-passive DR instead of weighted routing or custom Lambda automation.
docs.expected: Route 53 failover routing: primary record + health check, secondary record to the DR Region, allow health checkers through NACL/SG, Evaluate Target Health = Yes. Triggers: "route to DR only when primary fails", "warm standby", "automatically" → failover routing policy.
docs.why_not: Weighted sends traffic to both stacks continuously; EventBridge/CloudWatch + Lambda ChangeResourceRecordSets is custom code duplicating a native feature.

question.stem:
A company runs a messaging application in the `ap-northeast-1` and `ap-southeast-2` region. A Solutions Architect needs to create a routing policy wherein a larger portion of traffic from the Philippines and North India will be routed to the resource in the `ap-northeast-1` region.
Which Route 53 routing policy should the Solutions Architect use?
options: Geolocation Routing
Geoproximity Routing
Weighted Routing
Latency Routing
question.explanation: Geoproximity routing sends users to the geographically nearest resource and lets you apply a bias (+1..+99 expands a region's area, -1..-99 shrinks it). Raising the bias on ap-northeast-1 grows its catchment so that a larger portion of users in borderline areas like the Philippines and North India are routed there. Geolocation maps whole countries/continents to a resource (all-or-nothing per location, no 'larger portion'); Weighted splits all traffic by percentage regardless of where users are; Latency picks the lowest-latency Region and can't be tuned to shift a portion of traffic.

docs.concept: Route 53 geoproximity: bias to shift a larger share of traffic to a Region
docs.tests: Telling geoproximity (distance + adjustable bias) apart from geolocation (fixed mapping by country/continent), weighted and latency routing.
docs.expected: Geoproximity routing with a positive bias on ap-northeast-1. Triggers: "larger portion of traffic" from certain areas → shift the boundary → geoproximity + bias. "Users from country X must go to Y" would be geolocation.
docs.why_not: Geolocation — fixed country/continent → endpoint mapping, no proportional shift; Weighted — percentages for all users, ignores location; Latency — lowest latency only, not adjustable.

question.stem:
A digital media company shares static content to its premium users around the world and also to their partners who syndicate their media files. The company is looking for ways to reduce its server costs and securely deliver their data to their customers globally with low latency.
Which combination of services should be used to provide the MOST suitable and cost-effective architecture? (Select TWO.)
options: Amazon CloudFront
AWS Fargate
AWS Lambda
Amazon S3
AWS Global Accelerator
question.explanation: Static media files belong in Amazon S3 — durable, cheap object storage with no servers to run, which directly cuts server costs. Amazon CloudFront in front of S3 caches the files at edge locations worldwide for low latency and secures delivery with HTTPS, Origin Access Control (bucket stays private) and signed URLs/cookies for premium users and partners. Fargate and Lambda are compute — static content needs no compute. Global Accelerator speeds up TCP/UDP traffic to regional endpoints (ALB/NLB/EC2) via anycast IPs, but has no caching and can't use S3 as an endpoint.

docs.concept: CloudFront: global delivery of static content from an S3 origin
docs.tests: Choosing the serverless, cheapest architecture for global, secure, low-latency delivery of static content.
docs.expected: Amazon S3 (origin/storage) + Amazon CloudFront (CDN, HTTPS, OAC, signed URLs/cookies). Triggers: "static content", "globally", "low latency", "reduce server costs", "securely deliver to premium users/partners" → S3 + CloudFront.
docs.why_not: Fargate/Lambda are compute — Lambda can't store content or act as a CDN, and S3 is far cheaper than Fargate for static files; Global Accelerator is for non-HTTP (UDP gaming, IoT/MQTT, VoIP) or HTTP needing static IPs / fast regional failover, has no caching and no direct S3 integration.

question.stem:
All objects uploaded to an Amazon S3 bucket must be encrypted for security compliance. The bucket will use server-side encryption with Amazon S3-Managed encryption keys (SSE-S3) to encrypt data using 256-bit Advanced Encryption Standard (AES-256) block cipher.
Which of the following request headers must be used?
options: `x-amz-server-side-encryption-customer-algorithm`
`x-amz-server-side-encryption-customer-key`
`x-amz-server-side-encryption-customer-key-MD5`
`x-amz-server-side-encryption`
question.explanation: SSE-S3 is requested with the single header `x-amz-server-side-encryption: AES256` (for SSE-KMS the value is `aws:kms`, optionally with `x-amz-server-side-encryption-aws-kms-key-id`). The three `-customer-*` headers belong to SSE-C, where the client supplies its own key on every request: `-customer-algorithm` (AES256), `-customer-key` (base64 key) and `-customer-key-MD5` (integrity check of the key). Note: since 2023 S3 applies SSE-S3 by default to all new objects, but the header is still how a request explicitly asks for it (and what a bucket policy can enforce).

docs.concept: S3 encryption: request headers — SSE-S3 / SSE-KMS vs SSE-C
docs.tests: Knowing which PUT request header selects SSE-S3 versus the SSE-C customer-key headers.
docs.expected: `x-amz-server-side-encryption` with value `AES256`. Triggers: "SSE-S3", "S3-managed keys", "AES-256" → this header; anything with `-customer-` = SSE-C.
docs.why_not: All three `x-amz-server-side-encryption-customer-*` headers are for SSE-C (customer-provided key, algorithm and key MD5), not SSE-S3.

question.stem:
A solutions architect is designing a secure, cost-effective, and highly available storage solution for a company’s data. One of the requirements is to ensure that the previous version of a file is preserved and can be retrieved if a modified version is uploaded. Additionally, the company must comply with strict regulatory requirements that mandate data retention in an immutable state for at least 3 years before being moved to an archive. Once archived, the data will only be accessed once a year.
How should the solutions architect build the solution?
options: Create an Amazon S3 Standard bucket, enable object-level versioning, and then enable S3 Object Lock in compliance mode. After that, configure a lifecycle rule to move the files to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 3 years.
Create an Amazon S3 Standard bucket with object-level versioning enabled and configure a lifecycle rule that transfers files to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 3 years.
Create a One-Zone-IA bucket with object-level versioning enabled and configure a lifecycle rule that transfers files to Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 3 years.
Create an Amazon S3 Standard bucket and enable S3 Object Lock in governance mode.
question.explanation: Three requirements, three features: versioning keeps previous versions on overwrite; Object Lock in compliance mode makes versions immutable for the retention period (no one, including root, can delete or shorten it) — this is what 'strict regulatory' requires; a lifecycle rule moves data to Glacier Deep Archive after 3 years, the cheapest class for once-a-year access. Option 2 lacks immutability; option 3 uses One Zone-IA, which isn't highly available (single AZ) and also lacks Object Lock; option 4 uses governance mode (users with special permissions can bypass it — not strict compliance) and has no archiving.

docs.concept: S3 Object Lock: compliance mode (WORM, not even root can delete)
docs.tests: Combining S3 versioning, Object Lock compliance mode and a lifecycle transition to Deep Archive to meet version history, immutability and cheap archive requirements.
docs.expected: S3 Standard + versioning + Object Lock compliance mode + lifecycle to Glacier Deep Archive after 3 years. Triggers: "previous version preserved" → versioning; "strict regulatory / immutable" → Object Lock compliance; "accessed once a year" → Deep Archive; "highly available" → not One Zone-IA.
docs.why_not: Versioning + lifecycle alone isn't immutable; One Zone-IA isn't highly available and lacks WORM; governance mode can be bypassed with special permissions and there's no archive step.

question.stem:
An insurance company plans to implement a message filtering feature in its web application. To implement this solution, it needs to create separate Amazon SQS queues for each type of quote request. The entire message processing should not exceed 24 hours.
As the Solutions Architect for the company, which of the following solutions should be implemented to meet the above requirement?
options: Create a data stream in Amazon Kinesis Data Streams. Use the Kinesis Client Library to deliver all the records to the designated SQS queues based on the quote request type.

Create one Amazon SNS topic and configure the SQS queues to subscribe to the SNS topic. Set the filter policies in the SNS subscriptions to publish the message to the designated SQS queue based on its quote request type.
Create one Amazon SNS topic and configure the SQS queues to subscribe to the SNS topic. Publish the same messages to all SQS queues. Filter the messages in each queue based on the quote request type.
Create multiple Amazon SNS topics and configure the SQS queues to subscribe to the SNS topics. Publish the message to the designated SQS queue based on the quote request type.
question.explanation: SNS fan-out with subscription filter policies: the publisher sends every quote request to one topic with a message attribute (or body field) like quote_type; each SQS subscription has a filter policy (e.g. {"quote_type":["auto"]}) so SNS delivers only matching messages to that queue. No custom routing code, and SQS retention (default 4 days, up to 14) easily covers the 24-hour window. Kinesis + KCL means writing and running consumer code to route records — more overhead, and Kinesis isn't needed for simple routing. Publishing everything to all queues and filtering in each queue is impossible — SQS has no server-side filtering, so consumers would read and discard unwanted messages. Multiple topics push the routing logic back into the publisher and multiply resources to manage.

docs.concept: SNS: subscription filter policies route messages to specific SQS queues
docs.tests: Knowing that SNS subscription filter policies deliver only matching messages to each subscribed SQS queue, without custom routing code.
docs.expected: One SNS topic, SQS queues subscribed, a filter policy per subscription on the quote-type attribute. Triggers: "message filtering", "separate queue per type", fan-out → SNS + SQS with filter policies.
docs.why_not: Kinesis + KCL = custom routing code; SQS can't filter messages itself (consumers would discard); multiple topics push routing to the publisher and add resources.

question.stem:
An insurance company utilizes SAP HANA for its day-to-day ERP operations. Since it can’t migrate this database due to customer preferences, it needs to integrate it with the current AWS workload in the VPC, in which it is required to establish a site-to-site VPN connection.
What needs to be configured outside of the VPC for an AWS Virtual Private Network connection to succeed?
options: An Internet-routable IP address (static) of the customer gateway's external interface for the on-premises network
The main route table in your VPC to route traffic through a NAT instance
A dedicated NAT instance in a public subnet
An EIP to the Virtual Private Gateway
question.explanation: Outside the VPC, on the on-premises side, you need a customer gateway device whose external interface has a static, Internet-routable public IP (a device behind NAT can also work with NAT-T, but the classic exam answer is the static public IP). You register that IP as the Customer Gateway resource in AWS, and the IPsec tunnels are built between it and the two AWS tunnel endpoints of the Virtual Private Gateway. NAT instances and routing through them are inside the VPC and unrelated to VPN — VPN traffic uses a route to the VGW (or route propagation). The VGW's public tunnel endpoints are managed by AWS; you don't attach an Elastic IP to it.

docs.concept: Site-to-Site VPN: customer gateway needs a static public IP on-premises
docs.tests: Knowing the on-premises requirement for Site-to-Site VPN (customer gateway with an Internet-routable static IP) versus AWS-side components.
docs.expected: A static, Internet-routable public IP on the customer gateway's external interface. Triggers: "configured outside of the VPC", "site-to-site VPN" → customer gateway device with static public IP.
docs.why_not: NAT instance / main route table via NAT are inside the VPC and not part of VPN; the VGW's tunnel endpoints are AWS-managed — no Elastic IP is attached to it.

question.stem:
A global company has deployed numerous AWS Outposts servers in various remote locations worldwide. These servers frequently need to download software updates consisting of multiple files from an S3 bucket in the `us-west-2` region. The company is experiencing significant delays in distributing these updates across all servers.
What solution would most effectively reduce the deployment latency while minimizing operational overhead?
options: Set up AWS Global Accelerator to route traffic from Outposts servers to the nearest AWS edge location, then use private VIF connections to access the S3 bucket in `us-west-2`.
Use Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration on the existing S3 bucket and have the Outposts servers use the Transfer Acceleration endpoint for downloads.

Set up an Amazon CloudFront distribution with the `us-west-2` S3 bucket as the primary origin and create a secondary origin in another region, implementing a `CachingDisabled` cache policy. Use signed URLs for downloads.
Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution with the `us-west-2` S3 bucket as the origin. Use signed URLs for software downloads.
question.explanation: Many servers worldwide repeatedly download the same files → a CDN. CloudFront with the S3 bucket as origin caches the update files at edge locations near each Outpost; after the first request in a region the rest are served from the edge cache with low latency, and signed URLs keep the downloads private. It is fully managed — minimal overhead. S3 Transfer Acceleration speeds up individual transfers over the AWS backbone (mainly used for uploads) but has no caching, so every server still pulls every file from us-west-2. Global Accelerator doesn't support S3 as an endpoint and private VIFs require Direct Connect — complex and not applicable. CachingDisabled removes the whole point of CloudFront, and a secondary origin in another Region adds cross-Region replication to manage.

docs.concept: CloudFront: cache repeated downloads at the edge (vs S3 Transfer Acceleration)
docs.tests: Choosing CloudFront caching for many repeated global downloads of the same S3 objects, versus Transfer Acceleration, Global Accelerator or disabling caching.
docs.expected: CloudFront distribution with the S3 bucket as origin + signed URLs. Triggers: "many servers worldwide", "frequently download the same files", "reduce latency", "minimal overhead" → CloudFront caching.
docs.why_not: Transfer Acceleration has no cache (each download goes to us-west-2) and targets uploads; Global Accelerator can't front S3 and private VIF needs Direct Connect; CachingDisabled + secondary origin defeats caching and adds overhead.

question.stem:
A company has an on-premises MySQL database that needs to be replicated in Amazon S3 as CSV files. The database will eventually be launched on an Amazon Aurora Serverless cluster and accessed through an Amazon RDS Proxy endpoint to allow the web applications to pool and share database connections. Once data has been fully copied, the ongoing changes to the on-premises database should be continually streamed into the S3 bucket. The company wants a solution that can be implemented with little management overhead yet still highly secure.
Which ingestion pattern should a solutions architect take?
options: Set up a full load replication task using AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS). Launch a DMS endpoint with SSL using the AWS Network Firewall service.
Use AWS Schema Conversion Tool (AWS SCT) to convert MySQL data to CSV files. Set up the AWS Transform MGN to capture ongoing changes from the on-premises MySQL database and send them to S3.
Create a full load and change data capture (CDC) replication task using AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS). Add a new Certificate Authority (CA) certificate and create a DMS endpoint with SSL.
Use AWS DataSync to migrate data to S3 and AWS Data Transfer Terminal for ongoing changes. Create your own custom AWS KMS envelope encryption key for the associated DataSync job.
question.explanation: AWS DMS supports S3 as a target (CSV by default) and a 'full load + CDC' task type: it copies existing data, then continuously streams ongoing changes read from the MySQL binlog. For security, import the CA certificate into DMS and configure the source endpoint to use SSL, encrypting data in transit. 'Full load' only stops after the initial copy — no ongoing changes — and Network Firewall doesn't create SSL endpoints. SCT converts schemas between engines, it doesn't export data to CSV, and MGN replicates servers, not database changes to S3. DataSync moves files, not database changes, and Data Transfer Terminal is a physical location for uploading data from devices — neither does CDC.

docs.concept: DMS: full load + CDC to S3 with SSL endpoint
docs.tests: Choosing DMS full load + CDC to continuously replicate an on-prem database into S3, secured with an SSL endpoint (CA certificate).
docs.expected: DMS replication task of type full load + CDC, S3 target (CSV), source endpoint with SSL using an imported CA certificate. Triggers: "initial copy then ongoing changes continually streamed" → full load + CDC; "highly secure" → SSL endpoint.
docs.why_not: Full load only = no ongoing changes, Network Firewall doesn't do SSL endpoints; SCT converts schemas and MGN replicates servers; DataSync moves files and Data Transfer Terminal is a physical upload site — no CDC.

question.stem:
A company plans to migrate its suite of containerized applications running on-premises to a container service in AWS. The solution must be cloud-agnostic and use an open-source platform that can automatically manage containerized workloads and services. It should also use the same configuration and tools across various production environments.
What should the Solution Architect do to properly migrate and satisfy the given requirement?
options: Migrate the application to Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service with Amazon EKS worker nodes.
Migrate the application to Amazon Elastic Container Service with Amazon ECS tasks that use the Amazon EC2 launch type.
Migrate the application to AWS App Runner to run containers using an open‑source orchestration platform.
Migrate the application to Amazon Elastic Container Service with Amazon ECS tasks that use the AWS Fargate launch type.
question.explanation: 'Cloud-agnostic', 'open-source platform', 'same configuration and tools across environments' all point to Kubernetes. Amazon EKS runs upstream, CNCF-conformant Kubernetes, so the same manifests, Helm charts and kubectl tooling work on-premises, in other clouds and on AWS. ECS (EC2 or Fargate launch type) is AWS's proprietary orchestrator — task definitions and the ECS API don't exist outside AWS. App Runner is a proprietary fully managed service for web apps/APIs; it does not expose an open-source orchestration platform.

docs.concept: EKS: cloud-agnostic open-source Kubernetes vs proprietary ECS
docs.tests: Choosing EKS when the stem requires an open-source, cloud-agnostic orchestrator with the same tooling across environments.
docs.expected: Amazon EKS (with worker nodes / managed node groups or Fargate). Triggers: "cloud-agnostic", "open-source", "same configuration and tools across environments", "Kubernetes" → EKS.
docs.why_not: ECS (EC2 or Fargate launch type) is AWS-proprietary; App Runner is a proprietary managed service, not an open-source orchestrator.

question.stem:
A company hosts its web application on a set of Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB). The application has an embedded NoSQL database. As the application receives more traffic, the application becomes overloaded mainly due to database requests. The management wants to ensure that the database is eventually consistent and highly available.
Which of the following options can meet the company requirements with the least operational overhead?
options: Change the ALB with a Network Load Balancer (NLB) to handle more traffic. Use the AWS Glue DynamoDB export connector to export data from Amazon DynamoDB to Amazon S3 for analytics periodically, and continue running the application’s NoSQL database on the EC2 instances.

Change the ALB with a Network Load Balancer (NLB) to handle more traffic and integrate AWS Global Accelerator to ensure high availability. Configure replication of the NoSQL database on the set of EC2 instances to spread the database load.

Configure the Auto Scaling group to spread the EC2 instances across three Availability Zones. Use the AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) with a replication server and an ongoing replication task to migrate the embedded NoSQL database to Amazon DynamoDB.
Configure the Auto Scaling group to spread the EC2 instances across three Availability Zones. Configure replication of the NoSQL database on the set of EC2 instances to spread the database load.
question.explanation: The bottleneck is the database embedded in the web instances. Moving it to DynamoDB decouples the data tier: fully managed, auto-scaling, data replicated across 3 AZs, eventually consistent reads by default — highly available with no DB servers to run. DMS with an ongoing replication task migrates the data with minimal downtime, and spreading the ASG across 3 AZs makes the web tier highly available too. Swapping ALB for NLB doesn't fix database load, and exporting DynamoDB to S3 is irrelevant while the DB still runs on EC2. Self-managed replication of the NoSQL DB on EC2 (with or without Global Accelerator) keeps all the operational burden and the coupling of DB and web tier.

docs.concept: DynamoDB: offload an embedded NoSQL DB (DMS migration) for HA and scale
docs.tests: Decoupling an embedded database into managed DynamoDB (migrated with DMS ongoing replication) and multi-AZ ASG for HA with least overhead.
docs.expected: ASG across 3 AZs + DMS ongoing replication task to migrate the embedded NoSQL DB to DynamoDB. Triggers: "embedded NoSQL database overloaded", "eventually consistent", "highly available", "least operational overhead" → DynamoDB (via DMS).
docs.why_not: NLB swap doesn't reduce DB load and Glue export is irrelevant; self-managed NoSQL replication on EC2 (± Global Accelerator) keeps high ops overhead and couples DB with the web tier.

question.stem:
A company is running a dashboard application on a Spot EC2 instance inside a private subnet. The dashboard is reachable via a domain name that maps to the private IPv4 address of the instance’s network interface. A solutions architect needs to increase network availability by allowing the traffic flow to resume in another instance if the primary instance is terminated.
Which solution accomplishes these requirements?
options: Attach an elastic IP address to the instance’s primary network interface and point its IP address to the application’s domain name. Automatically move the EIP to a secondary instance if the primary instance becomes unavailable using the AWS Transit Gateway.

Create a secondary elastic network interface and point its private IPv4 address to the application’s domain name. Attach the new network interface to the primary instance. If the instance goes down, move the secondary network interface to another instance.
Use the AWS Network Firewall to detach the instance’s primary elastic network interface and move it to a new instance upon failure.

Set up AWS Transfer for FTPS service in Implicit FTPS mode to automatically disable the `source/destination` checks on the instance’s primary elastic network interface and reassociate it to another instance.
question.explanation: A secondary elastic network interface (ENI) is an independent resource: it keeps its private IPv4 address, MAC and security groups when detached, and can be attached to another instance in the same AZ. Pointing the domain name at the secondary ENI's private IP and moving that ENI to a standby instance on failure lets traffic resume without changing DNS. The primary ENI (eth0) can never be detached from an instance. An Elastic IP is a public address — useless for a private-IP domain in a private subnet — and Transit Gateway doesn't move EIPs. Network Firewall inspects traffic; it doesn't manage ENIs. AWS Transfer Family (FTPS) is a file-transfer service and has nothing to do with source/destination checks or ENIs.

docs.concept: EC2 ENI: move a secondary network interface to a standby instance for failover
docs.tests: Knowing that a secondary ENI keeps its private IP and can be moved between instances (same AZ) for failover, while the primary ENI can't be detached.
docs.expected: Create a secondary ENI, map the domain to its private IP, attach it to the primary instance, move it to another instance on failure. Triggers: "private IP in DNS", "resume traffic on another instance", "network availability" → movable secondary ENI.
docs.why_not: EIP is public and Transit Gateway doesn't move EIPs; primary ENI can't be detached (and Network Firewall doesn't manage ENIs); Transfer Family FTPS is unrelated to ENIs/source-dest checks.

question.stem:
An organization needs to control access to several Amazon S3 buckets. The organization plans to use a gateway endpoint to allow access to trusted buckets. The organization shall not use overly broad policies like `AmazonS3FullAccess`.
Which of the following could help achieve this requirement?
options: Generate a bucket policy for trusted S3 buckets.
Generate an endpoint policy for trusted S3 buckets.
Generate a bucket policy for trusted VPCs.
Generate an endpoint policy for trusted VPCs.
question.explanation: A VPC endpoint policy is a resource policy attached to the gateway endpoint that limits what can be accessed THROUGH that endpoint. Listing only the trusted bucket ARNs in its Resource element means instances in the VPC can reach those buckets via the endpoint and nothing else — a narrow allow-list instead of AmazonS3FullAccess. A bucket policy controls who can access that one bucket; it can't stop the VPC from reaching other, untrusted buckets through the endpoint, and you'd need one per bucket. 'Bucket policy for trusted VPCs' (aws:SourceVpc/aws:SourceVpce) restricts a bucket to certain VPCs — the inverse direction. An endpoint policy scopes resources/actions/principals, not 'trusted VPCs' — the endpoint already belongs to one VPC.

docs.concept: VPC endpoints: endpoint policy restricting which S3 buckets are reachable
docs.tests: Distinguishing a gateway endpoint policy (what the VPC can reach through the endpoint) from a bucket policy (who can reach the bucket).
docs.expected: An endpoint policy on the S3 gateway endpoint that allows only the trusted bucket ARNs. Triggers: "gateway endpoint" + "allow access only to trusted buckets" → endpoint policy with those buckets as Resource.
docs.why_not: Bucket policy governs access to one bucket, not what the VPC can reach elsewhere; bucket policy for trusted VPCs is the reverse direction; endpoint policies scope buckets/actions, not VPCs.

question.stem:
A company is building an internal application that allows users to upload images. Each upload request must be sent to Amazon Kinesis Data Streams for processing before the pictures are stored in an Amazon S3 bucket.
The application should immediately return a success message to the user after the upload, while the downstream processing is handled asynchronously. The processing typically takes about 5 minutes to complete.
Which solution will enable asynchronous processing from Kinesis to S3 in the most cost-effective way?
options: Send data from Kinesis Data Streams to Amazon Data Firehose and configure it to deliver directly to S3.
Use a combination of AWS Lambda and Step Functions to orchestrate service components and asynchronously process the requests.
Use a combination of Amazon SQS to queue the requests and then asynchronously process them using On-Demand Amazon EC2 Instances.
Use Kinesis Data Streams with AWS Lambda consumers to asynchronously process records and write them to S3.
question.explanation: The stream already exists; the app returns success as soon as the record is written to Kinesis. A Lambda function with the stream as an event source mapping polls the shards, processes each batch (5 minutes fits well within Lambda's 15-minute limit) and writes the result to S3 — serverless, pay per invocation, no idle cost. Firehose delivers (buffers and batches) data to S3 but isn't built for custom multi-minute processing — its optional transform Lambda is for light record transformation — so the required processing step isn't met. Step Functions adds an orchestration layer (and state-transition cost) that a single processing step doesn't need. SQS + On-Demand EC2 ignores the mandated Kinesis stream and pays for always-on instances.

docs.concept: Kinesis Data Streams + Lambda consumer: serverless async processing to S3
docs.tests: Choosing Lambda as a Kinesis consumer for asynchronous processing within 15 minutes, versus Firehose delivery, Step Functions or EC2.
docs.expected: Kinesis Data Streams with a Lambda consumer (event source mapping) that processes records and writes to S3. Triggers: "Kinesis already used", "asynchronous processing ~5 min" (< 15 min), "most cost-effective" → Lambda consumer.
docs.why_not: Firehose delivers/batches, not for custom 5-minute processing; Step Functions is unnecessary orchestration cost; SQS + On-Demand EC2 drops Kinesis and pays for idle servers.

question.stem:
A business has a network of surveillance cameras installed within the premises of its data center. Management wants to leverage Artificial Intelligence to monitor and detect unauthorized personnel entering restricted areas. Should an unauthorized person be detected, the security team must be alerted via SMS.
Which solution satisfies the requirement?
options: Configure Amazon Elastic Transcoder to stream live feeds from the cameras. Use Amazon Kendra to detect authorized personnel. Set the phone numbers of the security team as subscribers to an Amazon SNS topic.

Use Amazon Kinesis Video Streams to stream live feeds from the cameras. Use Amazon Rekognition to detect unauthorized personnel. Set the phone numbers of the security team as subscribers to an Amazon SNS topic.

Utilize a custom containerized video processing application on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS). Integrate AWS App2Container (A2C) and Amazon SageMaker Autopilot to detect unauthorized personnel. Set the phone numbers of the security team as subscribers to an Amazon SNS topic.

Set up Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus to stream live feeds from the cameras. Use Amazon Fraud Detector to detect unauthorized personnel. Set the phone numbers of the security team as subscribers to an Amazon SNS topic.
question.explanation: Kinesis Video Streams ingests live camera feeds; Rekognition Video analyzes the stream in real time and can search faces against a collection of authorized staff, flagging unknown people; results go to SNS, whose SMS subscribers (the security team's phone numbers) get the alert. Elastic Transcoder converts media files (no live streaming) and Kendra is document search. EKS + App2Container + SageMaker Autopilot means building and operating a custom pipeline — App2Container containerizes existing apps and Autopilot is AutoML for tabular data, not video. Managed Prometheus stores metrics, not video, and Fraud Detector scores online transactions.

docs.concept: Rekognition + Kinesis Video Streams: detect people in live video, alert via SNS
docs.tests: Matching live video ingestion (Kinesis Video Streams), image/video AI (Rekognition) and SMS alerting (SNS).
docs.expected: Kinesis Video Streams → Rekognition Video (face search vs authorized collection) → SNS topic with SMS subscribers. Triggers: "cameras / live video" → KVS; "detect people/faces" → Rekognition; "alert via SMS" → SNS.
docs.why_not: Elastic Transcoder converts files and Kendra searches documents; EKS + A2C + SageMaker Autopilot is a custom build with the wrong tools; Prometheus is metrics and Fraud Detector is transaction fraud.

question.stem:
A media company wants to ensure that the images it delivers through Amazon CloudFront are compatible across various user devices. The company plans to serve images in WebP format to user agents that support it and return to JPEG format for those that don’t. Additionally, the company wants to add a custom header to the response for tracking purposes.
As a solution architect, what approach would one recommend to meet these requirements while minimizing operational overhead?
options: Create multiple CloudFront distributions, each serving a specific image format (WebP or JPEG). Route incoming requests based on the User-Agent header to the respective distribution using Amazon Route 53.
Configure CloudFront behaviors to handle different image formats based on the User-Agent header. Use Lambda@Edge functions to modify the response headers and serve the appropriate format.

Implement an image conversion service on Amazon EC2 instances and integrate it with CloudFront. Use AWS Lambda functions to modify the response headers and serve the appropriate format based on the User-Agent header.
Generate a CloudFront response headers policy. Utilize the policy to deliver the suitable image format according to the User-Agent HTTP header in the incoming request.
question.explanation: Lambda@Edge runs code at CloudFront edge locations on viewer/origin request and response events: on the request it inspects User-Agent/Accept and rewrites the URI to the .webp or .jpg object (and the header can be part of the cache key so each variant is cached separately); on the response it adds the custom tracking header. Fully managed, no servers. Route 53 routes by DNS and never sees HTTP headers like User-Agent, and multiple distributions add management. An EC2 conversion fleet is operational overhead, and a regular Lambda can't sit inline in CloudFront. A response headers policy can add or override response headers (e.g. the tracking header, CORS, security headers) but cannot choose which image format to serve based on the request.

docs.concept: CloudFront Lambda@Edge: content negotiation by header + custom response header
docs.tests: Choosing Lambda@Edge for request-based content selection (WebP vs JPEG by User-Agent) and response header modification, vs response headers policy, Route 53 or EC2.
docs.expected: CloudFront behaviors + Lambda@Edge: on viewer/origin request pick WebP or JPEG from User-Agent/Accept, on response add the custom header. Triggers: "serve different content by User-Agent", "modify headers", "minimal overhead" → Lambda@Edge (CloudFront Functions for very light header-only logic).
docs.why_not: Route 53 can't see HTTP headers and multiple distributions add overhead; EC2 conversion service is heavy and plain Lambda isn't inline with CloudFront; response headers policy only adds/overrides headers, it can't choose the image format.

question.stem:
A solutions architect is designing a three-tier website that will be hosted on an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group fronted by an Internet-facing Application Load Balancer (ALB). The website will persist data to an Amazon Aurora Serverless DB cluster, which will also be used for generating monthly reports.
The company requires a network topology that follows a layered approach to reduce the impact of misconfigured security groups or network access lists. Web filtering must also be enabled to automatically stop traffic to known malicious URLs and to immediately drop requests coming from blacklisted fully qualified domain names (FQDNs).
Which network topology provides the minimum resources needed for the website to work?
options: Set up an Application Load Balancer deployed in a public subnet, then host the Auto Scaling Group of EC2 instances and the Aurora Serverless DB cluster in private subnets. Launch an AWS Network Firewall with the appropriate firewall policy to automatically stop traffic to known malicious URLs and drop requests coming from blacklisted FQDNs. Reroute your Amazon VPC network traffic through the firewall endpoints.

Set up an Application Load Balancer and a NAT Gateway deployed in public subnets. Launch the Auto Scaling Group of EC2 instances and Aurora Serverless DB cluster in private subnets. Directly integrate the AWS Network Firewall with the Application Load Balancer to automatically stop traffic to known malicious URLs and drop requests coming from blacklisted FQDNs.

Set up an Application Load Balancer in front of an Auto Scaling group of EC2 instances with an Aurora Serverless DB cluster to persist data. Launch a NAT Gateway in a public subnet to restrict external services from initiating a connection to the EC2 instances and immediately drop requests from unauthorized FQDNs. Deploy all other resources in private subnets.

Set up an Auto Scaling group of EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer with an Aurora Serverless DB cluster to store application data. Deploy all resources in a public subnet. Configure host-based routing to the Application Load Balancer to stop traffic to known malicious URLs and drop requests from blacklisted FQDNs.
question.explanation: Minimum working three-tier layout: only the internet-facing ALB sits in public subnets; the EC2 Auto Scaling group and Aurora Serverless live in private subnets. AWS Network Firewall is deployed into its own firewall subnets and VPC route tables are changed to send traffic through the firewall endpoints; its stateful rule groups do domain-list (FQDN) filtering and Suricata-compatible URL/threat blocking — an extra inspection layer independent of SGs/NACLs (defense in depth). Option 2 adds a NAT Gateway the website doesn't need and claims Network Firewall integrates directly with an ALB — it doesn't, it works through routing. A NAT Gateway (option 3) only provides outbound internet for private subnets; it does no filtering of FQDNs or URLs. Option 4 puts everything, including the database, in public subnets, and ALB host-based routing forwards by Host header — it's not a threat-filtering feature.

docs.concept: Network Firewall: layered VPC filtering (FQDN/URL) via route-table redirection
docs.tests: Designing a minimal three-tier VPC and adding AWS Network Firewall for FQDN/URL filtering as a defense-in-depth layer beyond SGs and NACLs.
docs.expected: ALB in public subnets, EC2 ASG + Aurora in private subnets, AWS Network Firewall in firewall subnets with VPC traffic routed through its endpoints. Triggers: "layered approach", "misconfigured SGs/NACLs", "malicious URLs", "blacklisted FQDNs" → Network Firewall.
docs.why_not: NAT Gateway isn't needed and Network Firewall doesn't attach to an ALB; NAT Gateway doesn't filter domains; public DB and ALB host-based routing are not security filtering.

question.stem:
A multinational company currently operates multiple AWS accounts to support its operations across various branches and business units. The company needs a more efficient and secure approach in managing its vast AWS infrastructure to avoid costly operational overhead.
To address this, they plan to transition to a consolidated, multi-account architecture while integrating a centralized corporate directory service for authentication purposes.
Which combination of options can be used to meet the above requirements? (Select TWO.)
options: Establish an identity pool through Amazon Cognito and adjust the AWS IAM Identity Center settings to allow Amazon Cognito authentication.
Integrate AWS IAM Identity Center with the corporate directory service for centralized authentication. Configure a service control policy (SCP) to manage the AWS accounts.
Utilize AWS CloudTrail to enable centralized logging and monitoring across all AWS accounts.
Set up a new entity in AWS Organizations and configure its authentication system to utilize AWS Directory Service directly.
Implement AWS Organizations to create a multi-account architecture that provides a consolidated view and centralized management of AWS accounts.
question.explanation: AWS Organizations provides the consolidated multi-account structure (OUs, consolidated billing, central management). IAM Identity Center connects to the corporate directory (via AD Connector / AWS Managed Microsoft AD or an external IdP) for single sign-on into all accounts, and SCPs set guardrails on the member accounts. Cognito identity pools are for application end users, and Identity Center does not accept Cognito as an identity source. CloudTrail centralizes auditing/logging but provides neither the multi-account structure nor directory authentication. Organizations has no built-in authentication system that 'directly uses Directory Service' — sign-in is handled by Identity Center.

docs.concept: IAM Identity Center + Organizations: multi-account SSO through existing AD (AD Connector)
docs.tests: Combining AWS Organizations (multi-account structure) with IAM Identity Center integrated with the corporate directory (+ SCPs) for centralized auth.
docs.expected: AWS Organizations for the multi-account architecture + IAM Identity Center integrated with the corporate directory and SCPs for guardrails. Triggers: "consolidated multi-account" → Organizations; "centralized corporate directory for authentication" → Identity Center.
docs.why_not: Cognito identity pools are for app users and aren't an Identity Center source; CloudTrail is logging, not structure/auth; Organizations has no own authentication to point at Directory Service.

question.stem:
For data privacy, a healthcare company has been asked to comply with the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA). The company stores all its backups on an Amazon S3 bucket. It is required that data stored on the S3 bucket must be encrypted.
What is the best option to do this? (Select TWO.)
options: Enable Server-Side Encryption on an S3 bucket to make use of AES-128 encryption.
Store the data in encrypted Amazon EBS snapshots.
Enable Server-Side Encryption on an S3 bucket to make use of AES-256 encryption.
Store the data on Amazon EBS volumes with encryption enabled instead of using S3.
Before sending the data to S3 over HTTPS, encrypt the data locally first using your own encryption keys.
question.explanation: Two valid ways to have S3 data encrypted at rest: server-side encryption, where S3 encrypts objects with AES-256 (SSE-S3; SSE-KMS also uses AES-256), and client-side encryption, where the data is encrypted locally with your own keys before upload (over HTTPS for in-transit protection) so S3 only ever stores ciphertext. S3 SSE doesn't use AES-128. EBS snapshots/volumes are a different storage service — the requirement is about the backups already in the S3 bucket, and moving them to EBS is costlier and less durable.

docs.concept: S3 encryption: SSE (AES-256) or client-side encryption
docs.tests: Knowing the two ways to encrypt data stored in S3 — server-side (AES-256) and client-side before upload — versus wrong key sizes or switching to EBS.
docs.expected: S3 server-side encryption with AES-256 (SSE-S3/SSE-KMS) and client-side encryption with your own keys before uploading over HTTPS. Triggers: "data on S3 must be encrypted", "HIPAA/compliance" → SSE (AES-256) or client-side.
docs.why_not: S3 SSE doesn't use AES-128; EBS snapshots/volumes change the storage service instead of encrypting the S3 backups.

question.stem:
A solutions architect is instructed to host a website that consists of HTML, CSS, and some Javascript files. The web pages will display several high-resolution images. The website should have optimal loading times and be able to respond to high request rates.
Which of the following architectures can provide the most cost-effective and fastest loading experience?
options: Upload the HTML, CSS, Javascript, and the images in a single bucket. Then enable website hosting. Create a CloudFront distribution and point the domain on the S3 website endpoint.
Host the website using an Nginx server in an EC2 instance. Upload the images in an S3 bucket. Use CloudFront as a CDN to deliver the images closer to end-users.
Host the website in an AWS Elastic Beanstalk environment. Upload the images in an S3 bucket. Use CloudFront as a CDN to deliver the images closer to your end-users.

Launch an Auto Scaling Group using an AMI that has a pre-configured Apache web server, then configure the scaling policy accordingly. Store the images in an Elastic Block Store. Then, point your instance’s endpoint to AWS Global Accelerator.
question.explanation: HTML, CSS, JS and images are all static, so no servers are needed: S3 static website hosting serves them at virtually unlimited request rates for cents, and CloudFront in front caches everything (pages and high-resolution images) at edge locations for the fastest load times. The EC2/Nginx and Elastic Beanstalk options run and pay for servers just to serve static files, and only images get the CDN. ASG + Apache + EBS + Global Accelerator is the most expensive, EBS can't be shared across instances, and Global Accelerator doesn't cache.

docs.concept: S3 + CloudFront + ACM: serverless static website
docs.tests: Recognizing a purely static website and choosing S3 website hosting + CloudFront over server-based options.
docs.expected: All static files in S3 with website hosting, CloudFront in front, domain pointed to CloudFront. Triggers: "HTML, CSS, JavaScript", "images", "high request rates", "cost-effective, fastest" → S3 + CloudFront, no servers.
docs.why_not: EC2/Nginx and Beanstalk pay for servers for static content; ASG + EBS + Global Accelerator is costliest, EBS isn't shared and GA has no cache.

question.stem:
A start-up company has an EC2 instance that is hosting a web application. The volume of users is expected to grow in the coming months and hence, you need to add more elasticity and scalability in your AWS architecture to cope with the demand.
Which of the following options can satisfy the above requirement for the given scenario? (Select TWO.)
options: Set up two EC2 instances and then put them behind an Elastic Load balancer (ELB).
Set up two EC2 instances deployed using Launch Templates and integrated with AWS Glue.
Set up an S3 Cache in front of the EC2 instance.
Set up two EC2 instances and use Route 53 to route traffic based on a Weighted Routing Policy.
Set up an AWS WAF behind your EC2 Instance.
question.explanation: Scalability here means horizontal scaling: run more than one instance and spread traffic across them. An ELB distributes requests across the instances (and with an Auto Scaling group behind it gives real elasticity). Route 53 weighted routing also spreads traffic across multiple instances at the DNS level (e.g. 50/50), optionally with health checks. AWS Glue is an ETL service — irrelevant to web scaling. 'S3 Cache' is not an AWS feature (caching in front of a web tier is CloudFront or ElastiCache). WAF filters malicious HTTP requests in front of ALB/CloudFront/API Gateway — it's security, not scaling, and it sits in front, not behind, and not on EC2 directly.

docs.concept: Scaling out a web tier: multiple EC2 behind ELB or Route 53 weighted
docs.tests: Recognizing horizontal scaling options (ELB, Route 53 weighted across instances) versus unrelated services (Glue, WAF) and non-existent features (S3 Cache).
docs.expected: Two+ EC2 instances behind an ELB, and two+ EC2 instances with Route 53 weighted routing. Triggers: "single EC2", "users will grow", "elasticity and scalability" → scale out and distribute traffic (ELB, ideally + Auto Scaling; or Route 53 weighted).
docs.why_not: Glue is ETL; 'S3 Cache' doesn't exist (CloudFront/ElastiCache do caching); WAF is a security filter placed in front of ALB/CloudFront/API Gateway, not a scaling tool.

question.stem:
A travel company has a suite of web applications hosted in an Auto Scaling group of On-Demand EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer that handles traffic from various web domains such as `i-love-manila.com`,`i-love-boracay.com` `i-love-cebu.com` and many others. To improve security and lessen the overall cost, you are instructed to secure the system by allowing multiple domains to serve SSL traffic without the need to reauthenticate and reprovision your certificate everytime you add a new domain. This migration from HTTP to HTTPS will help improve their SEO and Google search ranking.
Which of the following is the most cost-effective solution to meet the above requirement?
options: Add a Subject Alternative Name (SAN) for each additional domain to your certificate.
Use a wildcard certificate to handle multiple sub-domains and different domains.

Create a new CloudFront web distribution and configure it to serve HTTPS requests using dedicated IP addresses in order to associate your alternate domain names with a dedicated IP address in each CloudFront edge location.

Upload all SSL certificates of the domains in the ALB using the console and bind multiple certificates to the same secure listener on your load balancer. ALB will automatically choose the optimal TLS certificate for each client using Server Name Indication (SNI).
question.explanation: An ALB HTTPS listener can hold multiple certificates (a default plus additional ones) and uses Server Name Indication (SNI) to pick the right certificate for the domain the client requested, at no extra cost. Adding a domain is just attaching another certificate to the listener. A SAN certificate needs reissuing every time a domain is added, a wildcard certificate covers only subdomains of ONE domain (not different domains), and CloudFront with dedicated IPs costs about $600 per month per distribution.

docs.concept: ALB: multiple TLS certificates on one HTTPS listener via SNI
docs.tests: Serving many different domains over HTTPS from one ALB cheaply: attach multiple certificates to the listener and rely on SNI, versus SAN/wildcard certificates or CloudFront dedicated IP.
docs.expected: Bind multiple certificates (e.g. from ACM) to the same ALB HTTPS listener; the ALB picks the certificate with SNI. Triggers: 'multiple domains', 'without reprovisioning the certificate for each new domain', 'most cost-effective', 'ALB'.
docs.why_not: SAN means re-issuing the certificate for every new domain. A wildcard covers subdomains of one domain (*.example.com), not different domains. CloudFront with dedicated IPs is very expensive and unnecessary since SNI is free.

question.stem:
A large financial firm needs to set up a Linux bastion host to allow access to the Amazon EC2 instances running in their VPC. For security purposes, only the clients connecting from the corporate external public IP address 175.45.116.100 should have SSH access to the host.
Which is the best option that can meet the customer’s requirement?
options: Security Group Inbound Rule: Protocol – TCP. Port Range – 22, Source 175.45.116.100/32
Security Group Inbound Rule: Protocol – UDP, Port Range – 22, Source 175.45.116.100/32
Network ACL Inbound Rule: Protocol – UDP, Port Range – 22, Source 175.45.116.100/32
Network ACL Inbound Rule: Protocol – TCP, Port Range-22, Source 175.45.116.100/0
question.explanation: SSH runs over TCP port 22, and /32 limits the source to exactly one IP. A Security Group is stateful, so the return traffic is allowed automatically. UDP (options 2 and 3) is the wrong protocol for SSH. The NACL option with /0 is an invalid/wrong CIDR (/0 would mean any address) and a NACL is stateless, so it would also need an outbound rule for ephemeral ports.

docs.concept: Bastion host: public subnet + EIP, RDP/SSH only from corporate IPs
docs.tests: Writing the exact rule that restricts SSH to one corporate IP: right protocol (TCP 22), right CIDR (/32 = single host), and the right layer (Security Group, stateful).
docs.expected: Security Group inbound rule TCP 22 from 175.45.116.100/32. Triggers: 'Linux bastion', 'SSH', 'only from corporate public IP'.
docs.why_not: UDP 22 is the wrong protocol (SSH is TCP). NACL with /0 allows the entire internet, not one IP, and NACLs are stateless (return traffic needs its own outbound rule) — the SG is simpler and correct.

question.stem:
A company has established a dedicated network connection from its on-premises data center to AWS Cloud using AWS Direct Connect (DX). The core network services, such as the Domain Name System (DNS) service and Active Directory services, are all hosted on-premises. The company has new AWS accounts that will also require consistent and dedicated access to these network services.
Which of the following can satisfy this requirement with the LEAST amount of operational overhead and in a cost-effective manner?
options: Set up another Direct Connect connection for each and every new AWS account that will be added.
Create a new AWS VPN CloudHub. Set up a Virtual Private Network (VPN) connection for additional AWS accounts.
Set up a new Direct Connect gateway and integrate it with the existing Direct Connect connection. Configure a VPC peering connection between AWS accounts and associate it with Direct Connect gateway.
Create a new Direct Connect gateway and integrate it with the existing Direct Connect connection. Set up a Transit Gateway between AWS accounts and associate it with the Direct Connect gateway.
question.explanation: A Direct Connect gateway lets one DX connection reach VPCs in many accounts and Regions, and a Transit Gateway associated with it (via a transit VIF) fans out to all the account VPCs with transitive routing, so adding an account is just another TGW attachment. A DX connection per account is slow and expensive. VPN CloudHub uses internet-based VPNs, so it is not dedicated. VPC peering cannot be associated with a Direct Connect gateway (only a virtual private gateway or a Transit Gateway can) and peering is non-transitive.

docs.concept: Direct Connect Gateway + Transit Gateway: one DX connection shared by many accounts/VPCs
docs.tests: How to share one existing Direct Connect link with many (new) AWS accounts with the least overhead: Direct Connect gateway plus Transit Gateway (transit VIF), not more DX links, not VPN, not VPC peering.
docs.expected: Create a Direct Connect gateway, associate it with a Transit Gateway (shared to the other accounts, e.g. via RAM) that has the accounts' VPCs attached. Triggers: 'existing Direct Connect', 'new AWS accounts', 'consistent and dedicated access', 'least operational overhead'.
docs.why_not: A new DX per account is weeks of provisioning and costly. VPN CloudHub is over the internet (not dedicated/consistent). VPC peering cannot be associated with a Direct Connect gateway and is non-transitive, so on-prem could not reach the peered VPCs.

question.stem:
A company currently has an Augment Reality (AR) mobile game that has a serverless backend. It is using a DynamoDB table which was launched using the AWS CLI to store all the user data and information gathered from the players and a Lambda function to pull the data from DynamoDB. The game is being used by millions of users each day to read and store data.
How would you design the application to improve its overall performance and make it more scalable while keeping the costs low? (Select TWO)
options: Configure CloudFront with DynamoDB as the origin; cache frequently accessed data on the client device using ElastiCache.
Use AWS IAM Identity Center to authenticate users and have them directly access DynamoDB using single sign-on. Manually set the provisioned read and write capacity to a higher RCU and WCU.
Enable DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) and ensure that the Auto Scaling is enabled and increase the maximum provisioned read and write capacity.
Use API Gateway in conjunction with Lambda and turn on the caching on frequently accessed data and enable DynamoDB global replication.

Since Auto Scaling is enabled by default, the provisioned read and write capacity will adjust automatically. Also enable DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) to improve the performance from milliseconds to microseconds.
question.explanation: DAX gives microsecond reads for hot items, and DynamoDB Auto Scaling (explicitly enabled, with a higher max) absorbs traffic growth without over-provisioning. API Gateway with response caching in front of Lambda reduces Lambda/DynamoDB calls, and global tables bring data closer to players worldwide. CloudFront cannot use DynamoDB as an origin and ElastiCache is a server-side cache, not a device cache. Identity Center is for workforce SSO, not millions of game players, and manual capacity does not scale. The last option is wrong because Auto Scaling is NOT enabled by default for a table created with the AWS CLI/API (only the console default enables it).

docs.concept: DynamoDB: DAX for hot reads + auto scaling (CLI-created tables have none by default)
docs.tests: How to scale and speed up a serverless Lambda + DynamoDB backend cheaply: DAX cache, explicit Auto Scaling, API Gateway caching, global tables — and the trap that Auto Scaling is not on by default for tables created via CLI.
docs.expected: Pick DAX + explicitly enabled Auto Scaling (higher max capacity), and API Gateway caching in front of Lambda + DynamoDB global tables. Triggers: 'millions of users', 'read and store data', 'improve performance', 'keeping costs low', 'launched using the AWS CLI'.
docs.why_not: CloudFront can't front DynamoDB as an origin and ElastiCache doesn't run on client devices. IAM Identity Center is for workforce SSO, and manually raised capacity is static and costly. 'Auto Scaling is enabled by default' is false for CLI-created tables.

question.stem:
A FinTech startup deployed an application on an Amazon EC2 instance with attached Instance Store volumes and an Elastic IP address. The server is only accessed from 8 AM to 6 PM and can be stopped from 6 PM to 8 AM for cost efficiency using AWS Lambda with a script that automates this based on tags.
Which of the following will occur when the EC2 instance is stopped and started? (Select TWO.)
options: The Elastic IP address is disassociated with the instance.
The ENI (Elastic Network Interface) is detached.
The underlying host for the instance is possibly changed.
All data on the attached instance-store devices will be lost.
There will be no changes.
question.explanation: When an EBS-backed instance is stopped and started, it may be placed on a different underlying host, and data on instance-store volumes is lost (it lives on the host's disks). The Elastic IP stays associated with the instance, and the primary ENI stays attached (its private IP and MAC persist), so those options are wrong. 'No changes' is wrong because of the host change and instance-store loss.

docs.concept: EC2 stop/start: instance store data lost, host may change, Elastic IP and ENI persist
docs.tests: What survives an EC2 stop/start: EBS data, Elastic IP and primary ENI persist; instance-store data is lost and the instance may move to another host.
docs.expected: Host possibly changed and instance-store data lost. Triggers: 'Instance Store volumes', 'stopped and started', 'Elastic IP' (which persists).
docs.why_not: The Elastic IP stays associated across stop/start (it is only released if you disassociate/release it; a non-Elastic public IP would change). The primary ENI remains attached. 'No changes' ignores the host move and the instance-store wipe.

question.stem:
A company that is rapidly growing in recent months has been in the process of setting up IAM users on its single AWS Account. A solutions architect has been tasked to handle the user management, which includes granting read-only access to users and denying permissions whenever an IAM user has no MFA setup. New users will be added frequently based on their respective departments.
Which of the following action is the MOST secure way to grant permissions to the new users?
options: Launch an IAM Group for each department. Create an IAM Policy that enforces MFA authentication with the least privilege permission. Attach the IAM Policy to each IAM Group.
Create an IAM Role that enforces MFA authentication with the least privilege permission. Set up a corresponding IAM Group for each department. Attach the IAM Role to the IAM Groups.
Create a Service Control Policy (SCP) that enforces MFA authentication for each department. Add a trust relationship to every SCP and attach it to each IAM User.
Set up IAM roles for each IAM user and associate a permissions boundary that defines the maximum permissions.
question.explanation: Groups are the scalable way to manage many users by department: new users just join the group and inherit its policy. An IAM policy with an aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent condition (deny without MFA) plus read-only least-privilege permissions gives the required behavior. A role cannot be attached to a group (roles are assumed, not attached). SCPs apply to accounts/OUs in AWS Organizations, not to individual IAM users, and have no trust relationship. A role plus permissions boundary per user does not scale and a boundary only caps permissions, it grants none.

docs.concept: IAM: groups per department + MFA-enforcing policy (aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent)
docs.tests: Scalable, secure user management: attach a least-privilege policy with an MFA condition to IAM groups (per department), and know that roles can't be attached to groups and SCPs don't apply to individual IAM users.
docs.expected: An IAM group per department with an attached policy that grants read-only access and denies (or only allows with) aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent = true. New users are added to the group. Triggers: 'new users added frequently', 'per department', 'deny without MFA'.
docs.why_not: A role can't be attached to a group (users/services assume roles). SCPs work on accounts and OUs in Organizations, not on IAM users, and SCPs have no trust relationship. A role per user with a permissions boundary doesn't scale, and a boundary sets a maximum but grants nothing.

question.stem:
A company hosted a web application on a Linux Amazon EC2 instance in the public subnet that uses a non-default network ACL. The instance uses a default security group and has an attached Elastic IP address. The network ACL is configured to block all inbound and outbound traffic. The Solutions Architect must allow incoming traffic on port 443 to access the application from any source.
Which combination of steps will accomplish this requirement? (Select TWO.)
options: In the Network ACL, update the rule to allow both inbound and outbound TCP connection on port 443 from source `0.0.0.0/0` and to destination `0.0.0.0/0`
In the Security Group, create a new rule to allow TCP connection on port 443 to destination `0.0.0.0/0`
In the Network ACL, update the rule to allow inbound TCP connection on port 443 from source `0.0.0.0/0` and outbound TCP connection on port `32768 - 65535` to destination `0.0.0.0/0`
In the Security Group, add a new rule to allow TCP connection on port 443 from source `0.0.0.0/0`
In the Network ACL, update the rule to allow outbound TCP connection on port `32768 - 65535` to destination `0.0.0.0/0`
question.explanation: The Security Group needs an inbound rule for TCP 443 from 0.0.0.0/0 (default SG only allows traffic from itself); it is stateful, so replies are allowed automatically. The Network ACL is stateless: it needs an inbound allow for TCP 443 and an outbound allow for the ephemeral ports (32768-65535) that the client uses for the response. Allowing outbound port 443 is wrong because the reply goes to the client's ephemeral port, a SG rule 'to destination' is an outbound rule that is not needed, and the last option lacks the inbound 443 rule.

docs.concept: NACL: stateless — outbound rule for ephemeral ports
docs.tests: Opening HTTPS to the internet needs both layers: SG inbound 443 (stateful) and NACL inbound 443 plus outbound ephemeral ports (stateless).
docs.expected: Security Group: inbound TCP 443 from 0.0.0.0/0. Network ACL: inbound TCP 443 from 0.0.0.0/0 and outbound TCP 32768-65535 (ephemeral ports) to 0.0.0.0/0. Triggers: 'non-default network ACL blocks all', 'default security group', 'port 443 from any source'.
docs.why_not: NACL outbound 443 is wrong because the response leaves from 443 to the client's ephemeral port. A SG rule with a destination is outbound and unnecessary (SG is stateful, outbound already open by default). Outbound ephemeral alone lacks inbound 443.

question.stem:
A company runs a multi-tier web application in the AWS Cloud. The application tier is hosted on Amazon EC2 instances and the backend database is hosted on an Amazon Aurora for MySQL DB cluster. For security compliance, all of the application variables such as DB hostnames, environment settings, product keys, and database passwords must be stored securely with encryption.
Which of the following options is the most cost-effective solution to meet the requirements?
options: Store the values by creating secrets in AWS Secrets Manager. Use AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) for the encryption. Use the `BatchGetSecretValue` API to retrieve multiple secrets efficiently. Update the application to retrieve the values of the secrets.
