Store the values by creating SecureString type parameters in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store. Use AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) for the encryption. Update the application to retrieve the parameter values.
Store the values as key-value pairs in AWS Systems Manager OpsCenter. By default, the key-value pairs will be encrypted at rest. Configure the application to retrieve the variables when it starts.
Store the values in a file saved in an Amazon S3 bucket. Enable encryption on the S3 bucket. Configure the application to download the file contents when it starts.
question.explanation: Parameter Store SecureString parameters are KMS-encrypted and standard parameters are free, so it is the cheapest managed way to keep config values and secrets. Secrets Manager also works but charges per secret per month plus API calls, and nothing here needs automatic rotation. OpsCenter is an operations-issue (OpsItem) tool, not a configuration or secret store. An S3 file is not a secrets store: no per-value access control or auditing of reads, and it is easy to expose.

docs.concept: SSM Parameter Store: SecureString for cheap encrypted config and secrets (no rotation needed)
docs.tests: Choosing between Secrets Manager and Parameter Store SecureString: when only encrypted storage is required (no automatic rotation) and cost matters, Parameter Store is the answer.
docs.expected: SecureString parameters in Systems Manager Parameter Store, encrypted with KMS; the app reads them via the SSM API using its IAM role. Triggers: 'most cost-effective', 'variables, hostnames, passwords', no mention of rotation.
docs.why_not: Secrets Manager costs per secret and per API call and its main benefit (automatic rotation) is not required. OpsCenter is for operational issues (OpsItems), not for storing configuration. A file in S3 lacks secret-store features (fine-grained per-value access, audit, versioning semantics) and is a security anti-pattern.

question.stem:
A large insurance company has an AWS account that contains three VPCs (DEV, UAT and PROD) in the same region. UAT is peered to both PROD and DEV using a VPC peering connection. All VPCs have non-overlapping CIDR blocks. The company wants to push minor code releases from Dev to Prod to speed up time to market.
Which of the following options helps the company accomplish this?
options: Do nothing. Since these two VPCs are already connected via UAT, they already have a connection to each other.
Create a new VPC peering connection between PROD and DEV with the appropriate routes.
Create a new entry to PROD in the DEV route table using the VPC peering connection as the target.
Change the DEV and PROD VPCs to have overlapping CIDR blocks to be able to connect them.
question.explanation: VPC peering is non-transitive: DEV↔UAT and UAT↔PROD do not give DEV↔PROD. You need a direct DEV↔PROD peering connection (CIDRs are already non-overlapping) plus routes in both route tables. A route entry alone (option 3) has no peering connection to point to. Overlapping CIDRs (option 4) make peering impossible.

docs.concept: VPC Peering: non-transitive — VPCs that must talk need a direct peering plus routes on both sides
docs.tests: Whether you know VPC peering is non-transitive, so a shared middle VPC (UAT) gives no DEV↔PROD path, and what a working peering needs (connection + routes both ways + non-overlapping CIDRs).
docs.expected: Create a direct peering connection between DEV and PROD, accept it, and add routes to each other's CIDR in both route tables (and allow it in SGs/NACLs). Trigger words: 'UAT is peered to both', 'already connected via', 'non-overlapping CIDR'.
docs.why_not: 'Do nothing' assumes transitive routing, which peering does not support. A route entry alone has no peering connection to use as target (and would need one on both sides). Overlapping CIDRs are forbidden for peering and would break routing rather than enable it.

question.stem:
A company is generating confidential data that is saved on its on-premises data center. As a backup solution, the company wants to upload its data to an Amazon S3 bucket. In compliance with its internal security mandate, the encryption of the data must be done before sending it to S3. The company must spend time managing and rotating the encryption keys as well as controlling who can access those keys.
Which of the following methods can achieve this requirement? (Select TWO.)
options: Set up Client-Side Encryption with AWS KMS key.
Set up Server-Side Encryption with keys stored in a separate S3 bucket.
Set up Server-Side Encryption (SSE) with Amazon EC2 key pair.
Set up Client-Side Encryption with S3 managed encryption keys.
Set up Client-Side Encryption using a client-side master key.
question.explanation: Encryption before upload means client-side encryption. You can use a KMS key (you manage the key policy, rotation and who can use it) or a client-side master key that you keep and manage yourself. Server-side encryption happens after the data reaches S3, so it does not meet the requirement, and 'keys in a separate S3 bucket' and 'EC2 key pair' are not S3 encryption options. S3 managed keys (SSE-S3) are server-side and managed by AWS, so they cannot be used for client-side encryption and the company would not be managing them.

docs.concept: S3 client-side encryption: encrypt before upload with a KMS key or your own master key
docs.tests: Recognizing that 'encrypt before sending to S3' means client-side encryption, and that the keys can be a KMS key or a client-side master key, while SSE (server-side) and 'S3 managed keys' don't fit.
docs.expected: Client-side encryption using an AWS KMS key or a client-side master key. Triggers: 'encryption must be done before sending it to S3', 'manage and rotate the keys', 'control who can access those keys'.
docs.why_not: SSE happens after upload, so it fails 'before sending'. Keys in another S3 bucket and EC2 key pairs aren't S3 encryption options. S3 managed keys are SSE-S3, server-side and managed by AWS, so they don't fit client-side encryption or self-managed keys.

question.stem:
A company intends to give each of its developers a personal AWS account through AWS Organizations. To enforce regulatory policies, preconfigured AWS Config rules will be set in the new accounts. A solutions architect must see to it that developers are unable to remove or modify any rules in AWS Config.
Which solution meets the objective with the least operational overhead?
options: Use an IAM Role in the new accounts with an attached IAM trust relationship to disable the access of the root user to AWS Config.
Add the developers' AWS account to an organization unit (OU). Attach a service control policy (SCP) to the OU that restricts access to AWS Config.
Configure an AWS Config rule in the root account to detect if changes to the new account’s Config rules are made.

Set up an AWS Control Tower in the root account to detect if there were any changes to the new account’s AWS Config rules. Attach an IAM trust relationship to the IAM User of each developer which prevents any changes in AWS Config.
question.explanation: An SCP attached to the OU denies the AWS Config actions that modify or delete rules (e.g. config:DeleteConfigRule, config:PutConfigRule, config:StopConfigurationRecorder) for every account in the OU, including future ones and even for account admins and the root user of member accounts. It is a preventive control set once. A role trust policy cannot disable the root user. An AWS Config rule only detects and does not prevent. Control Tower detects changes, and IAM trust relationships attached to users are not a thing (trust policies belong to roles) and would be per-user overhead.

docs.concept: Organizations SCP: deny changes to AWS Config rules for all accounts in an OU
docs.tests: Preventive guardrail across many accounts: an SCP on the OU that denies AWS Config modification actions, versus detective controls (Config rule, Control Tower detection) or IAM trust policies.
docs.expected: Put the accounts in an OU and attach an SCP denying config:DeleteConfigRule, config:PutConfigRule, config:StopConfigurationRecorder etc. Triggers: 'unable to remove or modify', 'AWS Organizations', 'least operational overhead'.
docs.why_not: Trust policies belong to roles and can't disable the root user. A Config rule in the root account only detects changes after they happen. Control Tower detective controls don't prevent changes, and 'IAM trust relationship on a user' doesn't exist and would be per-user work.

question.stem:
A company needs to use Amazon Aurora as the Amazon RDS database engine for its web application. The Solutions Architect has been instructed to implement a 90-day RDS backup retention policy.
Which of the following options can satisfy the given requirement?
options: Create an AWS Backup plan to take daily snapshots with a retention period of 90 days.
Configure RDS to export the automated snapshot automatically to Amazon S3 and create a lifecycle policy to delete the object after 90 days.
Configure an automated backup and set the backup retention period to 90 days.
Create a daily scheduled event using Amazon EventBridge and AWS Lambda to directly download the RDS automated snapshot to an Amazon S3 bucket. Archive snapshots older than 90 days to Glacier.
question.explanation: RDS/Aurora automated backups keep a maximum of 35 days, so a 90-day retention needs AWS Backup: a backup plan with a daily rule and 90-day retention (fully managed, no code). Setting the automated backup retention to 90 days is not possible. Exporting snapshots to S3 is a manual/scripted export to Parquet that is not an automatic feature of automated backups and is not directly restorable. You cannot directly download RDS snapshots to S3 with a Lambda function.

docs.concept: RDS/Aurora backups: automated backups max 35 days, use AWS Backup for longer retention
docs.tests: Knowing the automated backup retention limit for RDS/Aurora (35 days) and that longer retention (e.g. 90 days) is done with AWS Backup plans (or manual snapshots).
docs.expected: An AWS Backup plan with a daily backup rule and a 90-day retention. Triggers: 'Aurora', '90-day backup retention', RDS automated backups top out at 35 days.
docs.why_not: Automated backup retention can't exceed 35 days, so option 3 can't be configured. S3 export is not an automatic feature of automated snapshots, produces Parquet files and is not a restorable backup. A Lambda can't just download an RDS snapshot to S3, and building this yourself is high overhead.

question.stem:
An online registration system hosted in an Amazon EKS cluster stores data to a `db.t4g.medium` Amazon Aurora DB cluster. The database performs well during regular hours but is unable to handle the traffic surge that occurs during flash sales. A solutions architect must move the database to Aurora Serverless while minimizing downtime and the impact on the operation of the application.
Which change should be taken to meet the objective?
options: Change the Aurora Instance class to Serverless
Take a snapshot of the DB cluster. Use the snapshot to create a new Aurora DB cluster.
Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) to migrate to a new Aurora Serverless database.
Add an Aurora Replica to the cluster and set its instance class to Serverless. Failover to the read replica and promote it to primary.
question.explanation: Aurora Serverless v2 instances can be added to an existing provisioned cluster. Add a Serverless v2 reader, then fail over so it is promoted to writer: the switch takes seconds, the endpoint stays the same and the data is never copied. Changing the instance class in place of the writer causes downtime (the instance is modified/rebooted). Snapshot-restore creates a new cluster with a new endpoint and loses the changes made after the snapshot. DMS works but is a heavier migration with extra setup and cutover effort for a move within Aurora.

docs.concept: Aurora: move provisioned to Serverless v2 by adding a Serverless reader and failing over
docs.tests: Low-downtime migration from provisioned Aurora to Serverless v2: add a Serverless v2 replica to the same cluster, fail over to it, no data migration needed.
docs.expected: Add an Aurora Serverless v2 reader instance to the cluster, then fail over to promote it to writer. Triggers: 'move to Aurora Serverless', 'minimizing downtime', 'traffic surge/flash sales'.
docs.why_not: Modifying the writer's instance class causes downtime. Snapshot + restore makes a new cluster (new endpoint, stale data, downtime to cut over). DMS is heavy machinery for a move inside Aurora.

question.stem:
A company is deploying a Microsoft SharePoint Server environment on AWS using CloudFormation. The Solutions Architect needs to install and configure the architecture that is composed of Microsoft Active Directory (AD) domain controllers, Microsoft SQL Server 2012, multiple Amazon EC2 instances to host the Microsoft SharePoint Server and many other dependencies. The Architect needs to ensure that the required components are properly running before the stack creation proceeds.
Which of the following should the Architect do to meet this requirement?
options: Configure the `DependsOn` attribute in the CloudFormation template. Send a success signal after the applications are installed and configured using the `cfn-init` helper script.
Configure a `UpdatePolicy` attribute to the instance in the CloudFormation template. Send a success signal after the applications are installed and configured using the `cfn-signal` helper script.
Configure the `UpdateReplacePolicy` attribute in the CloudFormation template. Send a success signal after the applications are installed and configured using the `cfn-signal` helper script.
Configure a `CreationPolicy` attribute to the instance in the CloudFormation template. Send a success signal after the applications are installed and configured using the `cfn-signal` helper script.
question.explanation: A CreationPolicy on the instance makes CloudFormation wait (up to a timeout) until it receives the required number of success signals sent by cfn-signal, so the stack doesn't proceed until the software is installed and running. DependsOn only orders resource creation and cfn-init installs/configures but doesn't signal. UpdatePolicy applies to stack updates (ASG/Lambda alias updates), and UpdateReplacePolicy controls what happens to the old resource on replacement during updates.

docs.concept: CloudFormation: CreationPolicy + cfn-signal to wait until instance software is ready
docs.tests: Making CloudFormation pause stack creation until an instance finishes bootstrapping: CreationPolicy on the resource plus cfn-signal from the instance (not DependsOn, UpdatePolicy or UpdateReplacePolicy).
docs.expected: Add a CreationPolicy (ResourceSignal Count/Timeout) to the instance or Auto Scaling group and call cfn-signal after setup succeeds. Triggers: 'ensure components are running before the stack creation proceeds', 'success signal', 'helper script'.
docs.why_not: DependsOn only orders creation, it doesn't wait for software readiness, and cfn-init doesn't send the signal. UpdatePolicy is for updates, not creation. UpdateReplacePolicy decides what happens to the old resource when it is replaced during an update.

question.stem: A company has clients all across the globe that access product files stored in several Amazon S3 buckets, which are behind each of the respective Amazon CloudFront web distributions. The company currently wants to deliver content to a specific client, ensuring that only that client can access the data. At present, all clients can access the S3 buckets directly using an S3 URL or through the CloudFront distribution. The Solutions Architect must serve the private content via CloudFront only, to secure the distribution of files. Which combination of actions should the Architect implement to meet the above requirements? (Select TWO.)
options: Require the users to access the private content by using special CloudFront signed URLs or signed cookies.
Restrict access to files in the origin by creating an origin access control (OAC) and giving it permission to read the files in the bucket.
Enable the Origin Shield feature of the CloudFront distribution to protect the files from unauthorized access.
Generate an S3 presigned URL to ensure that only the client can access the files. Remove permission to use S3 URLs to read the files for anyone else.
Create a custom CloudFront function to check and ensure that only their clients can access the files.
question.explanation: Two layers are needed. Signed URLs or signed cookies restrict WHO can fetch content through CloudFront (only clients holding a valid signature). An origin access control (OAC) with a bucket policy allowing only CloudFront removes direct S3 URL access, so CloudFront is the only path. Origin Shield is an extra caching layer, not security. An S3 presigned URL goes straight to S3 and bypasses CloudFront. A CloudFront Function is lightweight viewer-event logic and is not the standard way to authenticate specific clients.

docs.concept: CloudFront private content: signed URLs/cookies (who) + OAC (only via CloudFront)
docs.tests: Combining CloudFront signed URLs/cookies with OAC to serve private S3 content to specific clients only through CloudFront.
docs.expected: Signed URLs or signed cookies + OAC on the S3 origin with a bucket policy for CloudFront only. Triggers: 'only that client', 'serve private content via CloudFront only', 'clients can access S3 directly'.
docs.why_not: Origin Shield is an additional regional caching layer that reduces origin load and does not authenticate anyone. S3 presigned URL bypasses CloudFront and S3 access stays direct, which contradicts 'via CloudFront only'. CloudFront Function runs simple viewer-request code, it has no built-in per-client authorization and is not the answer for private content.

question.stem:
A Solutions Architect working for a startup is designing a High Performance Computing (HPC) application which is publicly accessible for their customers. The startup founders want to mitigate distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks on their application.
Which of the following options are not suitable to be implemented in this scenario? (Select TWO.)
options: Use an Amazon CloudFront service for distributing both static and dynamic content.
Add multiple Elastic Fabric Adapters (EFA) to each EC2 instance to increase the network bandwidth.
Use Dedicated EC2 instances to ensure that each instance has the maximum performance possible.
Use AWS Shield and AWS WAF.
Use an Application Load Balancer with Auto Scaling groups for your EC2 instances. Prevent direct Internet traffic to your Amazon RDS database by deploying it to a new private subnet.
question.explanation: DDoS mitigation relies on absorbing and filtering traffic at the edge and scaling: CloudFront for static and dynamic content, Shield and WAF, and an ALB with Auto Scaling in front of a database in a private subnet (reducing the attack surface). Elastic Fabric Adapters only speed up node-to-node HPC/ML traffic and do nothing against DDoS, and Dedicated Instances only give hardware isolation for the instances, they add no DDoS protection. Those two are the options that are not suitable.

docs.concept: DDoS mitigation: CloudFront + Shield + WAF + ALB/ASG + private subnets (EFA and Dedicated Instances don't help)
docs.tests: Recognizing which measures mitigate DDoS (edge distribution, Shield/WAF, load balancing with scaling, reduced attack surface) and which are performance/isolation features that don't (EFA, Dedicated Instances). Note the question asks for what is NOT suitable.
docs.expected: Not suitable: multiple EFAs (HPC network bandwidth) and Dedicated EC2 instances (hardware isolation). Suitable: CloudFront, Shield + WAF, ALB + Auto Scaling with RDS in a private subnet. Triggers: 'mitigate DDoS', 'not suitable' (inverted question).
docs.why_not: Reading the question inverted: CloudFront, Shield/WAF and ALB + ASG with a private database are valid DDoS mitigations. EFA is a network interface for tightly-coupled HPC/ML and Dedicated Instances are for hardware isolation/licensing, neither mitigates DDoS.

question.stem:
In Amazon EC2, you can manage your instances from the moment you launch them up to their termination. You can flexibly control your computing costs by changing the EC2 instance state.
Which of the following statements is true regarding EC2 billing? (Select TWO.)
options: You will be billed when your On-Demand instance is in `pending` state.
You will be billed when your Spot instance is preparing to stop with a `stopping` state.
You will be billed when your On-Demand instance is preparing to hibernate with a `stopping` state.
You will be billed when your Reserved instance is in `terminated` state.
You will not be billed for any instance usage while an instance is not in the `running` state.
question.explanation: On-Demand/Spot instances are not billed in `pending`, and a Spot instance that is stopping is not billed. An instance preparing to hibernate (`stopping`) is billed because it is still writing RAM to EBS. A Reserved Instance is billed for the whole reservation term even when the instance is `terminated`, since you pay for the reservation. So 'not billed while not running' is false.

docs.concept: EC2 billing by state: pending/stopped not billed; hibernate-stopping and Reserved Instances are billed
docs.tests: EC2 instance-state billing rules: running is billed, pending and stopped are not, stopping-to-hibernate is billed, and Reserved Instances bill through the term regardless of state.
docs.expected: Billed: instance preparing to hibernate (stopping) and Reserved Instance even when terminated. Not billed: pending, Spot stopping, stopped. Triggers: 'billing', 'instance state', 'hibernate', 'Reserved'.
docs.why_not: pending is not billed (instance is just starting). A stopping Spot instance isn't billed (only hibernate-stopping is, because of RAM-to-EBS writing). 'Not billed when not running' ignores hibernate-stopping and Reserved Instances.

question.stem:
A company plans to use a durable storage service to store on-premises database backups to the AWS Cloud. To move the backup data, the company needs a service that can store and retrieve objects via standard file storage protocols for quick recovery.
Which of the following options will meet this requirement?
options: Use AWS DataSync to directly transfer the backup data to Amazon S3 Glacier.
Use Amazon EBS volumes to store all the backup data and attach it to an Amazon EC2 instance.
Use the AWS Storage Gateway volume gateway to store the backup data and directly access it using Amazon S3 API actions.
Use the AWS Storage Gateway file gateway to store all the backup data in Amazon S3.
question.explanation: The Storage Gateway file gateway exposes NFS/SMB file shares on-premises and stores each file as an object in Amazon S3 (durable, and recent data is cached locally for quick recovery). DataSync is a transfer service, not a file protocol endpoint, and Glacier retrieval isn't quick. EBS volumes attach to EC2 in the cloud, not to on-premises servers. A volume gateway exposes iSCSI block volumes stored as EBS snapshots, so the data can't be accessed directly with S3 API actions.

docs.concept: Storage Gateway: File Gateway (NFS/SMB) stores files as S3 objects for on-premises backups
docs.tests: Mapping the access protocol to the right Storage Gateway type: NFS/SMB file storage backed by S3 = File Gateway (not Volume Gateway, DataSync or EBS).
docs.expected: AWS Storage Gateway file gateway: on-premises servers write backups over NFS/SMB and they land in S3 as objects. Triggers: 'standard file storage protocols', 'on-premises backups to S3', 'quick recovery'.
docs.why_not: DataSync moves data but isn't a file-protocol endpoint, and Glacier isn't a quick-recovery target. EBS attaches to EC2 instances, not on-premises servers. Volume gateway serves iSCSI block volumes stored as EBS snapshots, so objects can't be read via S3 API.

question.stem: An online stock trading application stores financial data in an Amazon S3 bucket, with a lifecycle policy that moves older data to Glacier every month. A strict compliance requirement mandates that a surprise audit can occur at any time, and the required data must be retrievable in under 15 minutes under all circumstances. The manager has instructed that retrieval capacity be available when needed and should support up to 150 MB/s of retrieval throughput. Which of the following will meet the given requirement? (Select TWO.)
options: Use Expedited Retrieval to access the financial data.
Use Bulk Retrieval to access the financial data.
Use Standard Retrieval for accessing the financial data.
Specify a range, or portion, of the financial data archive to retrieve.
Purchase provisioned retrieval capacity.
question.explanation: Expedited retrievals return data in 1-5 minutes, which fits the 15-minute limit. Expedited requests can be rejected when demand is high, so provisioned capacity units (each guarantees that expedited retrievals succeed and provides up to 150 MB/s) must be purchased to meet 'under all circumstances'. Bulk (5-12 h) and Standard (3-5 h) are too slow, and retrieving a byte range only reduces the amount of data and does not guarantee speed or capacity.

docs.concept: Glacier: Expedited retrieval + provisioned capacity guarantees fast retrieval
docs.tests: Guaranteeing Glacier retrieval in minutes: Expedited Retrieval combined with provisioned capacity units (150 MB/s each).
docs.expected: Expedited Retrieval + provisioned retrieval capacity. Triggers: 'under 15 minutes', 'under all circumstances', 'capacity available when needed', '150 MB/s'.
docs.why_not: Bulk Retrieval takes about 5-12 hours. Standard Retrieval takes about 3-5 hours. Retrieving a range of the archive saves cost and data volume but does not make retrieval faster or guaranteed.

question.stem:
A Data Analyst in a financial company is tasked to provide insights on stock market trends to the company’s clients. The company uses AWS Glue extract, transform, and load (ETL) jobs in daily report generation, which involves fetching data from an Amazon S3 bucket. The analyst discovered that old data from previous runs were being reprocessed, causing the jobs to take longer to complete.
Which solution would resolve the issue in the most operationally efficient way?
options: Enable job bookmark for the ETL job.
Parallelize the job by splitting the dataset into smaller partitions and processing them simultaneously using multiple EC2 instances.
Increase the size of the dataset used in the job to speed up the extraction and analysis process.

Create a Lambda function that removes any data already processed. Then, use Amazon EventBridge (Amazon CloudWatch Events) to trigger this function whenever the ETL job’s status switches to `SUCCEEDED`.
question.explanation: AWS Glue job bookmarks persist state between runs so the job processes only new or changed data, which stops the reprocessing of old data with a single setting and no extra code. Splitting the data across EC2 instances adds operational work and doesn't avoid processing old data. A bigger dataset makes the job slower. A Lambda that deletes processed data plus an EventBridge rule is custom machinery, risks deleting source data, and is less operationally efficient than a built-in feature.

docs.concept: Glue: job bookmarks to process only new data and avoid reprocessing
docs.tests: Knowing the built-in Glue feature that tracks already-processed data between runs: job bookmarks, instead of building custom cleanup or parallelization.
docs.expected: Enable job bookmark on the Glue ETL job so each run processes only new data. Triggers: 'old data from previous runs reprocessed', 'jobs take longer', 'operationally efficient'.
docs.why_not: Parallelizing on EC2 adds infrastructure and still reprocesses old data. A larger dataset only makes it slower. A Lambda + EventBridge cleanup is custom code that deletes source data and is higher overhead than the built-in bookmark.

question.stem:
A solutions architect is writing an AWS Lambda function that will process encrypted documents from an Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP file system. The documents are protected by an AWS KMS customer key. After processing the documents, the Lambda function will store the results in an S3 bucket with an Amazon S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval storage class. The solutions architect must ensure that the files can be decrypted by the Lambda function.
Which action accomplishes the requirement?
options: Attach the `kms:decrypt` permission to the Lambda function’s resource policy. Add a statement to the AWS KMS key’s policy that grants the function’s execution role the `kms:decrypt` permission.
Attach the `kms:decrypt` permission to the Lambda function’s resource policy. Add a statement to the AWS KMS key’s policy that grants the function’s resource policy ARN the `kms:decrypt` permission.
Attach the `kms:decrypt` permission to the Lambda function’s execution role. Add a statement to the AWS KMS key’s policy that grants the function’s ARN the `kms:decrypt` permission.
Attach the `kms:decrypt` permission to the Lambda function’s execution role. Add a statement to the AWS KMS key’s policy that grants the function’s execution role the `kms:decrypt` permission.
question.explanation: What the function is allowed to do is defined in its execution role (identity-based policy), so kms:Decrypt goes on the execution role. A KMS key is only usable when its key policy also allows the principal, so the key policy must name the execution role. A Lambda resource policy controls who can invoke the function, not what the function can call, and the function itself (its ARN) is not the principal making KMS calls; the execution role is.

docs.concept: KMS: Lambda needs kms:Decrypt on its execution role AND the key policy naming that role
docs.tests: Two-sided KMS authorization for a Lambda function: the execution role (identity policy) gets kms:Decrypt and the KMS key policy must allow that role; Lambda resource policies are for invoking.
docs.expected: Attach kms:Decrypt to the function's execution role and add a key policy statement allowing the execution role to decrypt. Triggers: 'Lambda function', 'KMS customer key', 'ensure the files can be decrypted'.
docs.why_not: A Lambda resource policy controls who may invoke the function, not which AWS services it can call, so kms:Decrypt there has no effect. A function ARN or resource policy ARN isn't the calling principal: Lambda calls KMS as its execution role, so the key policy must name the role.

question.stem:
A company is using Amazon VPC that has a CIDR block of 10.31.0.0/27 that is connected to the on-premises data center. There was a requirement to create a Lambda function that will process massive amounts of cryptocurrency transactions every minute and then store the results to EFS. After setting up the serverless architecture and connecting the Lambda function to the VPC, the Solutions Architect noticed an increase in invocation errors with EC2 error types such as EC2ThrottledException at certain times of the day.
Which of the following are the possible causes of this issue? (Select TWO.)
options: Your Lambda function exceeds the VPC quota for Elastic Network Interfaces (ENIs) or available IP addresses in the subnet.
The attached IAM execution role of your function does not have the necessary permissions to access the resources of your VPC.
Your VPC does not have a NAT gateway.
The Lambda function is placed in a VPC subnet with limited IP address capacity.
The associated security group of your function does not allow outbound connections.
question.explanation: A VPC-attached Lambda function uses ENIs in the subnet. Under peak load it needs more ENIs and IP addresses; a /27 subnet has only 27 usable IPs, and the ENI quota can also be hit. When capacity runs out, EC2 throttles the requests and invocations fail with EC2ThrottledException at busy times. Missing IAM permissions, a missing NAT gateway or a restrictive security group cause constant failures or timeouts, not periodic throttling.

docs.concept: Lambda in a VPC: ENI quota / subnet IP exhaustion causes EC2ThrottledException
docs.tests: Diagnosing periodic EC2ThrottledException errors for a VPC-attached Lambda function: ENI quota and subnet IP capacity.
docs.expected: Exceeded ENI quota or available IPs, and a subnet with limited IP capacity (small CIDR like /27). Fix: larger subnets in several AZs, request an ENI quota increase. Triggers: 'EC2ThrottledException', 'at certain times of the day', 'massive amounts', tiny CIDR.
docs.why_not: Execution role without VPC permissions gives a constant access error (EC2AccessDeniedException), not peak-time throttling. No NAT gateway affects internet access only, and EFS is reached over the private network. A security group blocking outbound traffic causes timeouts, not EC2 throttling.

question.stem:
A large financial firm in the country has an AWS environment that contains several Reserved EC2 instances hosting a web application that has been decommissioned last week. To save costs, you need to stop incurring charges for the Reserved instances as soon as possible.
What cost-effective steps will you take in this circumstance? (Select TWO.)
options: Stop the Reserved instances as soon as possible.
Terminate the Reserved instances as soon as possible to avoid getting billed at the on-demand price when it expires.
Contact AWS to cancel your AWS subscription.
Go to the Amazon.com online shopping website and sell the Reserved instances.
Go to the AWS Reserved Instance Marketplace and sell the Reserved instances.
question.explanation: Reserved Instances are a billing commitment for the term, so stopping the instance doesn't stop the charge. Terminate the instances so that once the reservation expires (or is sold) you aren't billed at on-demand rates, and sell the unused Reserved Instances on the AWS Reserved Instance Marketplace to recover part of the cost. Cancelling an 'AWS subscription' is not how RIs work and Amazon.com is not a place to sell RIs.

docs.concept: Reserved Instances: terminate the instances and sell unused RIs on the RI Marketplace
docs.tests: What to do with unneeded Reserved Instances: billing continues for the term, so terminate the instances and sell the reservation on the Reserved Instance Marketplace.
docs.expected: Terminate the instances (avoid on-demand billing after expiry) and sell the unused Reserved Instances on the AWS Reserved Instance Marketplace. Triggers: 'Reserved instances', 'decommissioned', 'stop incurring charges'.
docs.why_not: Stopping the instance doesn't stop RI billing (you pay for the reservation). You can't cancel an 'AWS subscription' to get out of RIs, and Amazon.com's shopping site doesn't buy Reserved Instances.

question.stem:
A company is hosting an application on EC2 instances that regularly pushes and fetches data in Amazon S3. Due to a change in compliance, the instances need to be moved on a private subnet. Along with this change, the company wants to lower the data transfer costs by configuring its AWS resources.
How can this be accomplished in the MOST cost-efficient manner?
options: Create an Amazon S3 interface endpoint to enable a connection between the instances and Amazon S3.
Set up a NAT Gateway in the public subnet to connect to Amazon S3.
Create an Amazon S3 gateway endpoint to enable a connection between the instances and Amazon S3.
Set up an AWS Transit Gateway to access Amazon S3.
question.explanation: An S3 gateway endpoint gives private-subnet instances a private path to S3 through a route table entry, with no internet gateway or NAT and at no additional charge. An interface endpoint also works but costs per hour and per GB. A NAT Gateway charges per hour and per GB processed. Transit Gateway connects VPCs and networks, it is not a way to reach S3.

docs.concept: VPC endpoints: S3/DynamoDB gateway endpoints instead of NAT (savings)
docs.tests: Cheapest private access from a private subnet to S3: the free S3 gateway endpoint (route table target), not NAT Gateway, interface endpoint or Transit Gateway.
docs.expected: Create an S3 gateway endpoint and associate it with the private subnets' route tables. Triggers: 'private subnet', 'S3', 'lower data transfer costs', 'MOST cost-efficient'.
docs.why_not: NAT Gateway costs per hour plus per GB processed. An interface endpoint (PrivateLink) is paid hourly and per GB and is not needed for S3 within the VPC. Transit Gateway interconnects networks, it doesn't provide S3 access.

question.stem:
A company has a global online trading platform in which users from all over the world regularly upload terabytes of transactional data to a centralized Amazon S3 bucket.
Which of the following should be used in the present system to improve throughput and ensure consistently fast data transfer to the S3 bucket, regardless of the user’s location?
options: AWS Direct Connect
S3 Transfer Acceleration
FTP
Use Amazon CloudFront Origin Access Control (OAC)
question.explanation: S3 Transfer Acceleration routes uploads from users anywhere to the nearest AWS edge location and then over the AWS backbone network to the bucket, giving fast, consistent upload speed for long-distance transfers; it is enabled on the bucket and used through the accelerate endpoint. Direct Connect is a dedicated link from one site, not from users worldwide. FTP is just a protocol with no acceleration. CloudFront OAC restricts bucket access to CloudFront and does not speed up uploads.

docs.concept: S3 Transfer Acceleration: fast uploads from distant users via edge locations
docs.tests: Choosing S3 Transfer Acceleration for fast, consistent uploads to one S3 bucket from users all over the world (vs Direct Connect, FTP or CloudFront OAC).
docs.expected: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the bucket and upload through the accelerate endpoint; combine with multipart upload for large files. Triggers: 'users from all over the world upload to a centralized S3 bucket', 'terabytes', 'consistently fast regardless of location'.
docs.why_not: Direct Connect is a private link from one data center or office, not a solution for global end users. FTP is a transfer protocol with no acceleration. CloudFront OAC is an access-control setting for serving private S3 content and does not speed up uploads.

question.stem:
A call center wants to use Artificial Intelligence(AI) to extract insights from audio recordings to assess the quality of its customer service. The calls are available in both English and Hindi. A sentiment analysis report in English must be generated for each recording to assess whether or not the customer had a positive experience. Once the solution is completed, new languages will eventually be supported, such as Arabic, Mandarin, and Spanish.
How can the solutions architect build the solution without maintaining any machine learning model?
options: Convert audio recordings into text using Amazon Transcribe. Set up Amazon Translate to translate Hindi texts into English and use Amazon Comprehend for sentiment analysis.

Transcribe audio recordings into text using Amazon Polly’s `StartSpeechSynthesisTask` operation. Set up Amazon Rekognition to recognize and automatically translate Hindi texts into English. Use the combination of Amazon Fraud Detector and Amazon SageMaker BlazingText algorithm for sentiment analysis.

Utilize the Amazon Lex service to convert audio recordings into text. Call the Amazon Translate API to translate Hindi texts into English and use Amazon SageMaker Clarify for sentiment prediction and analysis.

Set up Amazon Comprehend to convert audio recordings into text. Use Amazon Kendra to translate Hindi texts into English and utilize the Amazon Detective service to automatically detect negative user behaviors for sentiment analysis.
question.explanation: Transcribe converts speech to text (it supports many languages), Translate converts the Hindi text to English, and Comprehend performs sentiment analysis on the English text. All three are fully managed AI services, so no ML model has to be built or maintained, and new languages just need the corresponding language settings. Polly is text-to-speech and Rekognition analyzes images/video. Lex builds chatbots and SageMaker Clarify explains/bias-checks models, so you would maintain models. Comprehend does not transcribe audio, Kendra is enterprise search and Detective investigates security findings.

docs.concept: AI services: Transcribe (speech to text) + Translate + Comprehend (sentiment), no ML model to maintain
docs.tests: Matching managed AI services to each pipeline step: audio to text (Transcribe), language conversion (Translate), sentiment (Comprehend), and rejecting look-alike services (Polly, Rekognition, Lex, SageMaker, Kendra, Detective).
docs.expected: Transcribe the recordings, Translate Hindi text to English, then Comprehend for sentiment analysis. Triggers: 'audio recordings', 'sentiment analysis', 'translate', 'without maintaining any machine learning model'.
docs.why_not: Polly is text-to-speech and Rekognition is image/video analysis, and BlazingText/Fraud Detector don't fit. Lex builds chatbots (not transcription of recordings) and SageMaker Clarify is for model bias/explainability, which means custom models. Comprehend can't convert audio, Kendra is document search (not translation) and Detective is for security investigation.

question.stem:
A company has an Application Load Balancer (ALB) that accepts HTTP and HTTPS traffic on ports 80 and 443, respectively. Recently, the company associated a new domain for its website, and they want to ensure that all HTTP traffic for this new domain is automatically redirected to HTTPS to improve security.
Which ALB configuration should be done to satisfy the requirement?
options: Configure the existing HTTP listener to redirect traffic to port 443.
Configure the existing on port 443 and add a redirect action to HTTP on port 80.
Create a new HTTP listener on port 80 and add a redirect action to the HTTPS protocol on port 443.
Create a new ALB listener on port 443 and configure it to redirect HTTP traffic to HTTPS.
question.explanation: The ALB already has an HTTP listener on port 80, so the redirect is configured on that existing listener: a redirect action to HTTPS port 443 (HTTP 301), either as its default action or as a rule with a host-header condition for the new domain. A load balancer can have only one listener per port, so a second port-80 listener cannot be created. The HTTPS listener on 443 receives only HTTPS traffic, so a redirect there (to HTTP, or a new 443 listener) never sees the plain HTTP requests and would also downgrade security.

docs.concept: ALB HTTP to HTTPS redirect: redirect action on the existing port-80 listener
docs.tests: Knowing that HTTP-to-HTTPS redirection on an ALB is a redirect action (HTTP 301 to HTTPS:443) set on the existing HTTP:80 listener, and that one listener per port is allowed.
docs.expected: Edit the existing HTTP:80 listener: default action or a host-header rule with 'Redirect to HTTPS, port 443'. Triggers: 'redirect HTTP to HTTPS', 'ALB accepts HTTP and HTTPS on ports 80 and 443', 'new domain' (host condition).
docs.why_not: A new HTTP listener on port 80 is impossible because port 80 already has one (one listener per port). A redirect on the 443 listener never receives HTTP requests, and redirecting HTTPS to HTTP is the opposite of the goal. A new 443 listener would conflict with the existing one and still does not catch port-80 traffic.

question.stem: A tech company is currently using Auto Scaling for their web application. A new AMI now needs to be used for launching a fleet of EC2 instances. Which of the following changes needs to be done?
options: Create a new target group.
Do nothing. You can start directly launching EC2 instances in the Auto Scaling group with the same launch template.
Create a new launch template.
Create a new target group and launch template.
question.explanation: The AMI ID is defined in the launch template (or launch configuration) that the Auto Scaling group uses, and an existing template cannot be edited. To use a new AMI, create a new launch template (or a new version of it) and point the Auto Scaling group at it; new instances then launch from the new AMI. The target group is unrelated to the AMI, and the same unchanged template keeps launching the old AMI.

docs.concept: Auto Scaling: new AMI requires a new launch template (version)
docs.tests: Knowing that the AMI is part of the launch template, so a new AMI means a new launch template (version) attached to the Auto Scaling group.
docs.expected: Create a new launch template (or version) with the new AMI and update the Auto Scaling group. Existing instances are not replaced automatically (use instance refresh). Trigger: 'new AMI' for an Auto Scaling fleet.
docs.why_not: A new target group is about load balancer routing and has nothing to do with the AMI. Doing nothing keeps launching the old AMI because the template still references it. New target group plus template adds an unnecessary target group.

question.stem:
A food company bought 50 licenses of Windows Server to be used by developers when launching Amazon EC2 instances to deploy and test applications. The company recently adopted AWS Systems Manager Application Manager to group and monitor EC2-based workloads by team.
The developers are free to provision EC2 instances as long as a license is available. The licenses are tied to the total CPU count of each virtual machine. The company wants to ensure that developers won’t be able to launch new instances once the licenses are exhausted, and wants to receive notifications when all licenses are in use.
Which of the following options is the recommended solution to meet the company’s requirements?
options: Define licensing rules on AWS License Manager to track and control license usage. Enable the option to “Enforce license limit” to prevent going over the number of allocated licenses. Add an Amazon SNS topic to send notifications and alerts.

Upload the licenses on AWS Systems Manager Fleet Manager to be encrypted and distributed to EC2 instances. Attach an IAM role on the EC2 instances to request a license from the Fleet Manager. Set up an Amazon SNS to send notifications and alerts once all licenses are used.

Configure AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM) to track and control the licenses used by AWS resources. Configure AWS RAM to provide available licenses for EC2 instances. Set up an Amazon SNS to send notifications and alerts once all licenses are used.

Define license configuration rules on AWS Certificate Manager to track and control license usage. Enable the option to “Enforce certificate limit” to prevent going over the number of allocated licenses. Add an Amazon SQS queue with ChangeVisibility Timeout configured to send notifications and alerts.
question.explanation: AWS License Manager tracks software licenses (by vCPU, core, socket or instance count) for EC2 and on-premises servers. A license configuration with a license count and the 'Enforce license limit' option blocks launches of new instances once the limit is reached, and it can publish notifications to an SNS topic when usage hits a threshold. Fleet Manager is a Systems Manager console for managing servers and does not distribute licenses. RAM shares AWS resources between accounts and does not track license usage. AWS Certificate Manager issues TLS/SSL certificates, which have nothing to do with software licenses, and SQS is not a notification service.

docs.concept: AWS License Manager: track licenses and enforce the limit on EC2 launches
docs.tests: Choosing AWS License Manager (license configuration with 'Enforce license limit' + SNS) to cap launches when BYOL licenses are exhausted.
docs.expected: License Manager license configuration (count by vCPU/core/socket/instance), 'Enforce license limit' to block launches, SNS for threshold alerts. Triggers: 'licenses', 'won't be able to launch instances once exhausted', 'tied to CPU count', 'notifications when all licenses are in use'.
docs.why_not: Fleet Manager is a console for managing and remotely administering servers, it does not store or distribute licenses. RAM shares resources like subnets or Transit Gateways between accounts and has no license tracking. AWS Certificate Manager manages TLS certificates, not software licenses, and 'Enforce certificate limit' does not exist; SQS is a queue, not an alerting service.

question.stem:
A company hosts all its applications on its data center on the US East Coast. Most of the workloads are legacy applications that are hosted on individual virtual machines running in Linux and Windows operating systems. The company plans to migrate all of its VM workloads to the AWS cloud. To minimize changes in the applications during the migration process, it has been decided that the company will use a “lift-and-shift” strategy. The company also wants to minimize downtime during the migration process.
Which of the following options should the Solutions Architect implement for this scenario?
options: Utilize AWS DataSync to migrate the application workloads to AWS. Deploy the AWS DataSync VM on the on-premises data center. Once replication is completed, launch Amazon EC2 instances based on the created AMIs.
Export the on-premises VMs and upload the images to an Amazon S3 bucket. Use VM Import/Export service to import the images and launch them as Amazon EC2 instances.

Use the AWS Application Discovery Service for lift-and-shift migrations. Deploy the AWS Application Discovery Agent to the on-premises data center to start the replication process. After the replication task is completed, launch Amazon EC2 instances based on the created AMIs.

Install the AWS Replication Agent on each of the on-premises VMs to continuously replicate the servers to AWS. Use AWS Migration Service (AWS MGN) to launch test instances and perform cutover once testing is completed.
question.explanation: AWS Application Migration Service (MGN) is the recommended rehost (lift-and-shift) service. The AWS Replication Agent installed on each source server continuously replicates its disks to a staging area in AWS; you launch test instances, then perform the cutover, so downtime is limited to the final switch and the applications need no changes. DataSync moves files and cannot migrate whole servers. VM Import/Export is a one-time export, upload and import with no continuous replication, so downtime is long. Application Discovery Service only collects server inventory and utilization data and does not replicate anything.

docs.concept: AWS Application Migration Service (MGN): lift-and-shift with continuous replication and minimal downtime
docs.tests: Choosing AWS MGN with the Replication Agent for rehosting VMs to EC2 with minimal downtime, and telling it apart from DataSync, VM Import/Export and Application Discovery Service.
docs.expected: Install the AWS Replication Agent on each source server, replicate continuously, launch test instances, then cut over. Triggers: 'lift-and-shift', 'rehost', 'VMs', 'minimize downtime', 'minimize changes to the applications'.
docs.why_not: DataSync copies files and objects, not whole servers or OS disks. VM Import/Export is a one-time image import with no continuous replication, so the cutover downtime is long. Application Discovery Service only discovers and measures servers for planning, it has no replication and no migration function.

question.stem:
A company has hundreds of VPCs with multiple VPN connections to their data centers spanning 5 AWS Regions. As the number of its workloads grows, the company must be able to scale its networks across multiple accounts and VPCs to keep up. A Solutions Architect is tasked to interconnect all of the company’s on-premises networks, VPNs, and VPCs into a single gateway, which includes support for inter-region peering across multiple AWS regions.
Which of the following is the BEST solution that the architect should set up to support the required interconnectivity?
options: Set up an AWS Direct Connect Gateway to achieve inter-region VPC access to all of the AWS resources and on-premises data centers. Set up a link aggregation group (LAG) to aggregate multiple connections at a single AWS Direct Connect endpoint in order to treat them as a single, managed connection. Launch a virtual private gateway in each VPC and then create a public virtual interface for each AWS Direct Connect connection to the Direct Connect Gateway.
Set up an AWS Transit Gateway in each region to interconnect all networks within it. Then, route traffic between the transit gateways through a peering connection.

Enable inter-region VPC peering that allows peering relationships to be established between multiple VPCs across different AWS regions. Set up a networking configuration that ensures that the traffic will always stay on the global AWS backbone and never traverse the public Internet.

Set up an AWS VPN CloudHub for inter-region VPC access and a Direct Connect gateway for the VPN connections to the on-premises data centers. Create a virtual private gateway in each VPC, then create a private virtual interface for each AWS Direct Connect connection to the Direct Connect gateway.
question.explanation: AWS Transit Gateway is the hub that connects VPCs, VPNs and Direct Connect (through a Direct Connect gateway) with transitive routing and scales to thousands of attachments. A Transit Gateway is Regional, so with 5 Regions you deploy one per Region and connect them with Transit Gateway peering attachments, which gives inter-Region connectivity over the AWS backbone. VPC peering is a one-to-one, non-transitive link, so hundreds of VPCs would need a full mesh. A Direct Connect gateway (with VGWs and a public virtual interface, which is not even valid for this) and VPN CloudHub do not interconnect hundreds of VPCs across Regions.

docs.concept: Transit Gateway per Region + TGW peering: interconnect hundreds of VPCs, VPNs and Regions
docs.tests: Choosing Transit Gateways (one per Region, joined by TGW peering) to interconnect hundreds of VPCs, VPNs and on-premises networks across Regions, instead of VPC peering, Direct Connect gateway or VPN CloudHub.
docs.expected: One Transit Gateway per Region, VPCs and VPNs attached to it, Transit Gateways peered across Regions (static routes), shared with RAM across accounts. Triggers: 'hundreds of VPCs', 'single gateway', 'multiple accounts', 'inter-Region peering', 'VPN connections'.
docs.why_not: A Direct Connect gateway connects on-premises to VPCs through VGWs and does not give VPC-to-VPC transitive routing; a public virtual interface is also the wrong type for private VPC access. Inter-Region VPC peering is non-transitive and one-to-one, so hundreds of VPCs mean a huge full mesh, not a single gateway. VPN CloudHub links branch offices through one VGW in a hub-and-spoke VPN, it is not an inter-Region VPC fabric and is not combined with a Direct Connect gateway this way.

question.stem:
A company has a regional API Gateway in the us-east-2 region that serves as a proxy to a backend service. Clients connect to the service using the invoke URL of the API stage. To improve usability, the company wants to associate a custom domain name (api.tutorialsdojo.com) with the API. Moreover, the domain name must support HTTPS to ensure secure connections. The company has an existing hosted zone for its domain on Amazon Route 53.
Which of the following would be the next step to achieve the company’s objective?
options: Request a public certificate in the us-east-2 region for api.tutorialsdojo.com using AWS Certificate Manager (ACM). Create a regional API Gateway domain name and associate it with api.tutorialsdojo.com and the ACM certificate. In Route 53, create an alias record for api.tutorialsdojo.com that points to the API Gateway domain name.

Import an existing public certificate for api.tutorialsdojo.com into AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) in the us-east-2. In Route 53, create a CNAME record for api.tutorialsdojo.com that points to the invoke URL of the API Gateway stage.

Request a public certificate in the us-east-1 region for api.tutorialsdojo.com using AWS Certificate Manager (ACM). Create a regional API Gateway domain name and associate it with api.tutorialsdojo.com and the ACM certificate. In Route 53, create an alias record for api.tutorialsdojo.com that points to the API Gateway domain name.
Use the AWS Certificate Manager Private Certificate Authority (ACM PCA) to generate a private certificate for api.tutorialsdojo.com. Override the invoke URL using stage variables.
question.explanation: For a regional API Gateway endpoint the ACM certificate must be in the same Region as the API (us-east-2); only edge-optimized APIs (which use CloudFront) need the certificate in us-east-1. The steps are: request the public ACM certificate, create the API Gateway custom domain name (regional) with that certificate, map the API stage to it with a base path mapping, and create a Route 53 alias record pointing to the regional domain name that API Gateway returns. The us-east-1 certificate cannot be used for a regional domain in us-east-2. Importing a certificate and using a CNAME to the invoke URL does not attach the custom domain to the API (the TLS certificate would not match the invoke URL host). A private CA certificate is not trusted by public clients, and stage variables do not change the invoke URL.

docs.concept: API Gateway custom domain: regional endpoint needs an ACM certificate in the same Region, plus a Route 53 alias
docs.tests: Knowing where the ACM certificate must live for a regional API Gateway custom domain (same Region; us-east-1 only for edge-optimized and CloudFront) and that DNS uses an alias record to the API Gateway domain name.
docs.expected: ACM public certificate in the API's Region, regional custom domain name with a base path mapping to the stage, Route 53 alias A record to the API Gateway domain name. Triggers: 'regional API Gateway', 'custom domain name', 'HTTPS', 'Route 53 hosted zone'.
docs.why_not: A certificate in us-east-1 only works for edge-optimized APIs (CloudFront) and CloudFront itself, not for a regional endpoint in us-east-2. A CNAME to the invoke URL does not create a custom domain on the API, and an imported certificate is not auto-renewed. A private certificate from ACM PCA is not trusted by public clients, and stage variables never override the invoke URL.

question.stem:
A company has a team of developers that provisions its own resources on the AWS cloud. The developers use IAM user access keys to automate resource provisioning and application testing processes in AWS. To ensure proper security compliance, the security team wants to automate the process of deactivating and deleting any IAM user access key that is over 90 days old.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational effort?
options: Use the AWS Config managed rule to check if the IAM user access keys are not rotated within 90 days. Create an Amazon EventBridge rule for the non-compliant keys, and define a target to invoke a custom AWS Lambda function to deactivate and delete the keys.
Create an Amazon EventBridge rule to filter IAM user access keys older than 90 days. Define a target to invoke an AWS Lambda function to deactivate and delete the old access keys.
Create an Amazon EventBridge rule to filter IAM user access keys older than 90 days. Schedule an AWS Batch job that runs every 24 hours to delete all the specified access keys.
Create a custom AWS Config rule to check the max-age of IAM access keys. Use Amazon EventBridge Scheduler to invoke an AWS Batch job every 24 hours to delete all non-compliant access keys.
question.explanation: The AWS Config managed rule access-keys-rotated already checks whether IAM access keys are older than a set number of days (90), so nothing has to be written to detect old keys. Config emits compliance-change events to EventBridge, and an EventBridge rule on NON_COMPLIANT results invokes a small Lambda function that deactivates and deletes the key (Config can also run SSM Automation remediation). EventBridge cannot filter keys by age because IAM does not emit an event when a key becomes 90 days old, so those two options have no detection source. A custom Config rule plus Batch adds code and infrastructure you do not need when a managed rule exists.

docs.concept: Config managed rule access-keys-rotated + EventBridge + Lambda to remove old IAM access keys
docs.tests: Using the AWS Config managed rule (access-keys-rotated) as the detector and EventBridge + Lambda (or SSM Automation remediation) as the automatic response for IAM keys older than 90 days, with the least effort.
docs.expected: Config managed rule access-keys-rotated (maxAccessKeyAge 90) → EventBridge rule on NON_COMPLIANT → Lambda that deactivates then deletes the key. Triggers: 'access keys over 90 days', 'automate', 'LEAST operational effort'.
docs.why_not: An EventBridge rule alone cannot filter keys by age, because no event is emitted when a key reaches 90 days, so there is nothing to match. Batch jobs on a 24-hour schedule are extra infrastructure for a task a small Lambda does. A custom Config rule is unnecessary when a managed rule already checks access-key age.

question.stem:
A new company policy requires IAM users to change their passwords’ minimum length to 12 characters. After a random inspection, you found out that there are still employees who do not follow the policy.
How can you automatically check and evaluate whether the current password policy for an account complies with the company password policy?
options: Create a CloudTrail trail. Filter the result by setting the attribute to “Event Name” and lookup value to “ChangePassword”. This easily gives you the list of users who have made changes to their passwords.
Configure AWS Config to trigger an evaluation that will check the compliance for a user’s password periodically.

Create a rule in the Amazon CloudWatch event. Build an event pattern to match events on IAM. Set the event name to “ChangePassword” in the event pattern. Configure SNS to send notifications to you whenever a user has made changes to his password.
Create a Scheduled Lambda Function that will run a custom script to check compliance against changes made to the passwords periodically.
question.explanation: AWS Config continuously evaluates resource configuration against rules. The managed rule iam-password-policy checks whether the account password policy meets requirements such as minimum length (12) and reports compliant or non-compliant with no code to write. CloudTrail and CloudWatch/EventBridge events on ChangePassword only show that a user changed a password, they do not tell whether it meets the policy length. A scheduled Lambda would need a custom script to write and maintain, which is not the automatic managed check the question asks for.

docs.concept: AWS Config managed rule iam-password-policy checks the account password policy for compliance
docs.tests: Knowing that AWS Config (managed rule iam-password-policy) evaluates compliance with a password policy, while CloudTrail and EventBridge only record ChangePassword events.
docs.expected: AWS Config managed rule iam-password-policy with parameters (MinimumPasswordLength 12, etc.), periodic or change-triggered evaluation, compliance shown per account. Triggers: 'automatically check and evaluate', 'complies with the policy', 'password policy'.
docs.why_not: CloudTrail only logs the ChangePassword API call (who and when), it never evaluates the password against a policy. An EventBridge rule on ChangePassword just sends a notification for each change with no compliance check. A scheduled Lambda with a custom script could work but is custom code to maintain, while a managed Config rule exists.

question.stem:
A leading IT consulting company has an application which processes a large stream of financial data by an Amazon ECS Cluster then stores the result to a DynamoDB table. You have to design a solution to detect new entries in the DynamoDB table then automatically trigger a Lambda function to run some tests to verify the processed data.
What solution can be easily implemented to alert the Lambda function of new entries while requiring minimal configuration change to your architecture?
options: Invoke the Lambda functions using SNS each time that the ECS Cluster successfully processed financial data.
Use CloudWatch Alarms to trigger the Lambda function whenever a new entry is created in the DynamoDB table.
Enable DynamoDB Streams to capture table activity and automatically trigger the Lambda function.
Use Systems Manager Automation to detect new entries in the DynamoDB table then automatically invoke the Lambda function for processing.
question.explanation: DynamoDB Streams records item-level changes (inserts, updates, deletes) in order for 24 hours, and a Lambda function can be attached as an event source mapping that is invoked automatically for new records. It only needs the stream enabled on the table and a mapping to the function, with no change to the ECS application. The SNS option requires changing the ECS application code. CloudWatch alarms watch metric thresholds, not individual new items. Systems Manager Automation runs operational runbooks and does not watch DynamoDB for new entries.

docs.concept: DynamoDB Streams + Lambda event source mapping: react to new items with minimal changes
docs.tests: Choosing DynamoDB Streams with a Lambda trigger to react to table changes, instead of changing the producer, CloudWatch alarms or Systems Manager.
docs.expected: Enable DynamoDB Streams (new image / new and old images) and add the Lambda function as a trigger (event source mapping). Triggers: 'detect new entries in the DynamoDB table', 'automatically trigger a Lambda', 'minimal configuration change'.
docs.why_not: Invoking Lambda from SNS means modifying the ECS application to publish on every write, which is the opposite of minimal change. CloudWatch alarms evaluate metrics against thresholds, they cannot fire per new item. Systems Manager Automation executes runbooks and does not monitor table changes.

question.stem:
A solutions architect is tasked with designing a scalable infrastructure solution for a business that runs uses Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) to execute container applications. Since the company’s workload varies throughout the day, they want to make sure that its underlying infrastructure automatically scales in and out in response to demand.
Which of the following would meet the requirements with the LEAST amount of operational overhead?
options: Set up CloudWatch alarms for CPU utilization or request count to monitor the relevant metrics of the container applications running on Amazon EKS.
Use a combination of Kubernetes Metrics and Kubernetes Cluster Autoscaler to manage the number of nodes.
Integrate an edge-optimized API endpoint in Amazon API Gateway with Amazon EKS to manage and expose APIs for the containerized applications running on EKS.
Use Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling Groups with custom scaling policies to manage the scaling of EKS worker nodes.
question.explanation: The Kubernetes Metrics Server collects resource usage and the Kubernetes Cluster Autoscaler automatically adds nodes (through the node group's Auto Scaling group) when pods cannot be scheduled and removes under-used nodes, so the infrastructure follows demand with no custom scaling policies to build. CloudWatch alarms only monitor and notify, they do not scale anything by themselves. API Gateway exposes APIs and has nothing to do with scaling nodes. Managing EC2 Auto Scaling groups with custom policies works but is manual and the Auto Scaling group does not know about pending pods, so it is more operational work than the Cluster Autoscaler.

docs.concept: EKS: Kubernetes Metrics Server + Cluster Autoscaler scale the worker nodes automatically
docs.tests: Knowing that the Cluster Autoscaler (with the Metrics Server; HPA for pods) is the low-overhead way to scale EKS worker nodes in and out, versus CloudWatch alarms, API Gateway or hand-built Auto Scaling policies.
docs.expected: Metrics Server + Cluster Autoscaler (or Karpenter) for nodes, Horizontal Pod Autoscaler for pods; Fargate profiles remove node management entirely. Triggers: 'EKS', 'scales in and out', 'underlying infrastructure', 'least operational overhead'.
docs.why_not: CloudWatch alarms only alert, they do not add or remove nodes. API Gateway only publishes APIs and has no scaling role for the nodes. A custom EC2 Auto Scaling group policy has to be designed and tuned by hand and is not aware of pending pods, so it is more overhead than the Cluster Autoscaler.

question.stem:
A data analytics company, which uses machine learning to collect and analyze consumer data, is using Redshift cluster as their data warehouse. You are instructed to implement a disaster recovery plan for their systems to ensure business continuity even in the event of an AWS region outage.
Which of the following is the best approach to meet this requirement?
options: Do nothing because Amazon Redshift is a highly available, fully-managed data warehouse which can withstand an outage of an entire AWS region.
Use Automated snapshots of your Redshift Cluster.
Create a scheduled job that will automatically take the snapshot of your Redshift Cluster and store it to an S3 bucket. Restore the snapshot in case of an AWS region outage.
Enable Cross-Region Snapshots Copy in your Amazon Redshift Cluster.
question.explanation: A Redshift cluster runs in one Region (Multi-AZ exists only for RA3 and does not cover a Region outage). For Region-level disaster recovery, enable cross-Region snapshot copy so that automated and manual snapshots are copied automatically to a second Region, where you can restore a new cluster during an outage. Doing nothing leaves no recovery path, automated snapshots stay in the same Region (and are stored in S3 managed by Redshift), and a hand-made scheduled snapshot job to S3 still stays in the source Region and is custom work.

docs.concept: Redshift DR across Regions: enable cross-Region snapshot copy
docs.tests: Knowing that Region-outage protection for a Redshift cluster comes from cross-Region snapshot copy (restore in the other Region), not from the cluster's own availability or same-Region snapshots.
docs.expected: Enable cross-Region snapshot copy (with a retention period; use a KMS grant for encrypted clusters) and restore the cluster from the copied snapshot in the destination Region. Triggers: 'Redshift', 'disaster recovery', 'AWS Region outage'.
docs.why_not: A cluster is a single-Region resource, so it does not survive a Region outage by itself. Automated snapshots stay in the same Region and do not help when the Region is down. A custom scheduled snapshot job to S3 stays in the same Region unless copied, and it duplicates a built-in feature.

question.stem:
A financial firm is designing an application architecture for its online trading platform that must have high availability and fault tolerance. Their Solutions Architect configured the application to use an Amazon S3 bucket located in the us-east-1 region to store large amounts of intraday financial data. The stored financial data in the bucket must not be affected even if there is an outage in one of the Availability Zones or if there’s a regional service failure.
What should the Architect do to avoid any costly service disruptions and ensure data durability?
options: Create a Lifecycle Policy to regularly backup the S3 bucket to Amazon Glacier.
Enable Cross-Region Replication.
Copy the S3 bucket to an EBS-backed EC2 instance.
Create a new S3 bucket in another region and configure Cross-Account Access to the bucket located in us-east-1.
question.explanation: S3 already stores objects redundantly across several AZs in a Region, which covers an AZ outage. To survive a Region-wide failure, enable Cross-Region Replication (versioning is required on both buckets) so every new object is copied automatically to a bucket in another Region. A lifecycle rule moving data to Glacier stays in the same Region and is for cost, not DR. Copying to an EBS-backed EC2 instance is manual, small-scale and also in one Region. A second bucket with cross-account access only grants permissions, it does not copy any data.

docs.concept: S3 Cross-Region Replication protects data from a regional failure (AZ resilience is built in)
docs.tests: Knowing S3 is already multi-AZ, and that surviving a Region failure needs Cross-Region Replication (versioning on both buckets), not lifecycle transitions, EC2 copies or cross-account access.
docs.expected: Enable versioning on source and destination buckets, then configure a CRR rule (optionally RTC for a 15-minute SLA). Triggers: 'outage of an AZ or a regional service failure', 'S3 bucket', 'data durability'.
docs.why_not: A lifecycle policy to Glacier stays in the same Region and only changes storage class for cost. Copying to an EC2 instance's EBS volume is manual, size-limited and single-Region. A bucket in another Region with cross-account access only permits access, it does not replicate the data.

source.origin: user-supplied practice question (missed); category 'CSAA – Design Resilient Architectures'; the security group screenshot was not included, the MS SQL rule is assumed open to a wide source

question.stem:
A newly hired Solutions Architect is checking all of the security groups and network access control list rules of the company’s AWS resources. For security purposes, the MS SQL connection via port 1433 of the database tier should be secured. Below is the security group configuration of their Microsoft SQL Server database: [screenshot of the security group rules, not included]
The application tier hosted in an Auto Scaling group of EC2 instances is the only identified resource that needs to connect to the database. The Architect should ensure that the architecture complies with the best practice of granting least privilege.
Which of the following changes should be made to the security group configuration?
options: For the MS SQL rule, change the Source to the static AnyCast IP address attached to the application tier.
For the MS SQL rule, change the Source to the security group ID attached to the application tier.
For the MS SQL rule, change the Source to the EC2 instance IDs of the underlying instances of the Auto Scaling group.
For the MS SQL rule, change the Source to the Network ACL ID attached to the application tier.
question.explanation: A security group rule can use another security group as its Source. Setting the database rule's Source to the application tier's security group allows port 1433 only from instances that carry that group, so it keeps working as the Auto Scaling group adds and replaces instances and follows least privilege. A security group source cannot be an instance ID, a network ACL ID, and an application tier of EC2 instances has no 'AnyCast' IP address (anycast IPs belong to Global Accelerator), and fixed IPs would break as instances change.

docs.concept: Security group rule source = another security group (SG reference) for least privilege with Auto Scaling
docs.tests: Restricting a database port to the application tier by referencing the application tier's security group as the rule source, instead of IPs, instance IDs or NACL IDs.
docs.expected: Edit the inbound rule (TCP 1433) and set Source = the app tier's security group ID. Triggers: 'only the application tier needs to connect', 'Auto Scaling group', 'least privilege', 'security group'.
docs.why_not: AnyCast static IPs belong to Global Accelerator, EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group do not have one, and IP-based sources break when instances are replaced. Instance IDs are not valid security group sources and change with scaling. A network ACL ID cannot be a source: NACLs work on CIDR ranges at the subnet level and are not referenced by security groups.

question.stem:
A startup is planning to set up and govern a secure, compliant, multi-account AWS environment in preparation for its upcoming projects. The IT Manager requires the solution to have a dashboard for continuous detection of policy non-conformance and non-compliant resources across the enterprise, as well as to comply with the AWS multi-account strategy best practices.
Which of the following offers the easiest way to fulfill this task?
options: Launch new AWS member accounts using the AWS CloudFormation StackSets. Use AWS Config to continuously track the configuration changes and set rules to monitor non-compliant resources. Set up a Multi-Account Multi-Region Data Aggregator to monitor compliance data for rules and accounts in an aggregated view

Use AWS Service Catalog to launch new AWS member accounts. Configure AWS Service Catalog Launch Constraints to continuously track configuration changes and monitor non-compliant resources. Set up a Multi-Account Multi-Region Data Aggregator to monitor compliance data for rules and accounts in an aggregated view

Establish connectivity to AWS through an AWS Direct Connect Partner to securely link on-premises environments to the new AWS accounts. Use AWS Organizations to manage and govern multiple accounts. Set up AWS Config to monitor non-compliant resources across the enterprise.

Use AWS Control Tower to launch a landing zone to automatically provision and configure new accounts through an Account Factory. Utilize the AWS Control Tower dashboard to monitor provisioned accounts across your enterprise. Set up preventive and detective guardrails for policy enforcement.
question.explanation: AWS Control Tower is the easiest way to set up and govern a secure multi-account environment that follows AWS best practices: it creates a landing zone (built on Organizations, IAM Identity Center, CloudTrail and Config), provisions new accounts through Account Factory, applies preventive (SCP) and detective (Config) guardrails, and shows compliance status and non-compliant resources in its dashboard. The other options assemble the same pieces by hand (StackSets, Service Catalog, Config aggregators, Organizations) with much more setup, and Service Catalog launch constraints only define the IAM role used to launch products, they do not monitor compliance. Direct Connect is unrelated to account governance.

docs.concept: AWS Control Tower: landing zone, Account Factory, guardrails and a compliance dashboard for multi-account governance
docs.tests: Choosing AWS Control Tower as the easiest, best-practice way to set up and govern a multi-account environment with guardrails and a dashboard of non-compliant resources, versus hand-built StackSets/Config/Service Catalog combinations.
docs.expected: Control Tower landing zone + Account Factory + preventive/detective guardrails + dashboard. Triggers: 'set up and govern a secure, compliant, multi-account environment', 'dashboard for non-conformance', 'multi-account best practices', 'easiest way'.
docs.why_not: StackSets + Config + aggregator builds the governance by hand and has no account vending baseline or dashboard of guardrails. Service Catalog launch constraints only set the role used to deploy a product, they do not track configuration changes or compliance.
